real.title: Dependency strings are re-emitted with naive double-quote wrapping; any dependency value containing a quote (env markers) round-trips to invalid TOML and crashes `haute init`
real.description: Line 264 parses the dependency array slice with tomllib, producing UN-escaped Python strings (e.g. `pkg ; python_version < "3.11"`). Line 269 then re-emits each entry as `f'    "{dep}",\n'` — wrapping in a basic TOML string WITHOUT re-escaping embedded double quotes. So a dependency value that legitimately contains `"` (environment markers such as `"tomli ; python_version < \"3.11\""`, or URLs) is written back as `"pkg ; python_version < "3.11"",`, which is no longer valid TOML. The subsequent re-parse at `_ensure_haute_dependency` line 312 fails with `Unclosed array`, and `haute init` exits 1 with a raw traceback. Environment-marker dependencies with quotes are extremely common in real pyproject files, so this is a high-likelihood, high-impact corruption path. The fix is to emit each dep with a proper TOML string serializer (escape `\` and `"`, or use a TOML writer) rather than an f-string.
real.evidence: Repro output: `[rewrite] produced array region:  |     "tomli ; python_version < "3.11"",` then `[rewrite] rewritten text is INVALID TOML: Unclosed array (at line 8, column 32)` and `[init-path] _ensure_haute_dependency raised: Unclosed array (at line 8, column 32)`. Line 264 decodes the marker to the literal Python string `tomli ; python_version < "3.11"`; line 269 `"".join(f'    "{dep}",\n' ...)` re-emits it with unescaped embedded quotes, so the re-parse at _ensure_haute_dependency line 312 (`tomllib.loads(text)`) raises TOMLDecodeError.
real.fix: In `_rewrite_project_dependencies` (src/haute/cli/_init_cmd.py:269), stop building array entries with the naive `f'    "{dep}",\n'`. Serialize each dependency as a proper TOML basic string: escape backslash then double-quote (`dep.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"')`) before wrapping, or emit via a TOML writer (e.g. tomli-w) / json.dumps on the string (TOML basic-string escaping is a superset-compatible subset of JSON string escaping for these ASCII cases). Add a regression test that injects a dependency containing an environment marker like `tomli ; python_version < "3.11"` and asserts the rewritten file both re-parses as TOML and preserves the original marker dependency verbatim.

real.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1199-1221 (infer_v2_schema_from_data column assembly; the object-table branch `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` at :1213) interacting with the reserved sentinel `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF` (:72) consumed in shred_to_buffers._walk at :629-632
real.title: A literal JSON key named "$value" collides with the reserved scalar-array sentinel, so inference emits a $value-leaf column on an OBJECT table and shred_to_buffers silently drops EVERY record of that table
real.description: The module reserves the leaf token `$value` (`_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`) to mean "the scalar element itself" for scalar-array child tables, and the header comment (lines 70-71) asserts "a JSON key can't be `$value` in this path grammar, so there's no collision with a real field." That assertion is false. `infer_v2_schema_from_data` builds an object column's path as `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with NO escaping/guarding of `col_name`, so a record carrying a real key `"$value"` yields an object-table column with path `$[*].$value`. At shred time `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `$value`, which EQUALS `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`. In `shred_to_buffers._walk`, `is_scalar_table = any(leaf == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF ...)` (line 629) then becomes TRUE for what is actually an OBJECT table, so the shape guard `if is_scalar_table != (not is_dict)` (line 630) treats every dict record as a shape mismatch and `continue`s past it (counting it as a skipped row). The whole table emits ZERO rows. Because validate_v2_schema accepts `$value` as a legal leaf and `_v2_fingerprint` sees a distinct path, the cache is judged valid/fresh; the only signal is the skipped-rows counter (which the user must notice). This is distinct from the catalogued 'scalar-value-column-fixed-name-ambiguity' finding (that is about output-port identity / a real field named `value` being indistinguishable downstream); here the *sentinel* `$value` causes total, silent row loss on the build path.
real.evidence: Repro output: `inferred root column paths: {'$value': '$[*].$value', 'other': '$[*].other'}`; `parsed leaf: '$value' | sentinel: '$value'`; `root buffer row count: 0`; `skip stats: {'records': 0, 'rows_by_table': {'$[*]': 2}}`; `built root row_count: 0`; `loaded root frame height: 0 columns: ['$value', 'other']`. Two source records produce ZERO rows on the OBJECT root table, with a clean build (fingerprint=8dcd0756, cache judged valid). Code-trace confirms: shred_to_buffers._walk line 629 `is_scalar_table = any(leaf == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF ...)` is True for a dict record, so line 630 `is_scalar_table != (not is_dict)` = `True != False` = True -> _count_row_skip + continue for every record. No guard in validate_v2_schema (_api_input_schema.py:263-403), parse_column_path (:224-255), or infer_v2_schema_from_data (_json_shred.py:1210-1221) rejects or escapes a literal `$value` key; grep over src/haute confirms the sentinel `$value` is unguarded everywhere it is used.
real.fix: The header comment at _json_shred.py:70-71 asserting "a JSON key can't be `$value` in this path grammar" is false — `parse_column_path` happily returns `$value` for a real key. Make the collision impossible to express silently, consistent with the codebase's fail-loud rule: in `validate_v2_schema`, after parsing each column's leaf, raise `ApiInputSchemaError` if `leaf == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF` AND the table is not a pure scalar child table (i.e. it has any other column, or its sole column's name is not the reserved `value` scalar column). Equivalently/more robustly, reject any `$`-prefixed leaf key in `parse_column_path` so a literal `$value` key is a loud schema error rather than a silent total row-drop. Add a failing test first: records=[{"$value":10,"other":1},{"$value":20,"other":2}] -> assert the build/validate raises (or, if the design chooses to support such keys, that all rows are emitted) rather than silently yielding a 0-row frame. The deeper, fully-correct fix is to encode the scalar-array leaf with a marker outside the legal key space so a real key can never alias it.

real.title: compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar can emit a sidecar that expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar then rejects (write/read asymmetry)
real.description: Because the compact-write key normaliser (`_canonical_sidecar_key`, line 201) does NOT apply the int-like float-string migration while the expand-read normaliser (`_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`, line 225) DOES, two distinct row-array labels that differ only in float-string formatting (e.g. '5.' and '5', or '25.0' and '25') are written by `_compact_entry_rows`/`_insert_entry_value` as two distinct, non-colliding map keys (no duplicate raised on the write side). When that same compact sidecar is later loaded, `_expand_entries_map.walk` migrates both '5.' and '5' to '5' and raises a collision ValueError. The result is a save operation that SUCCEEDS but produces a JSON sidecar that can never be loaded again -- the pipeline becomes un-parseable until the user hand-edits the file. The two normalisation helpers are contradictory contracts for the same key space.
real.evidence: Repro (exit 0) output: WRITE side `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar({band:'5.'/value:1.0, band:'5'/value:2.0})` succeeds, compact_map = {'5.': 1.0, '5': 2.0} (two distinct top-level keys, no duplicate raised). READ side `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` on that SAME map raises: "ratingStep tables[0].entries factor 'band' compact key '5' collides with existing key '5.' after legacy key migration to '5'". Root-cause helpers disagree: `_canonical_sidecar_key('5.')`=='5.' (WRITE) vs `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key('5.')`=='5' (READ). Asymmetry is systematic, also hitting natural pairs ('25.0','25') and ('1e1','10').
real.fix: Make the write and read key normalisers symmetric so the round-trip is stable/loud. `_canonical_sidecar_key` (src/haute/_rating_step_config.py:44, used by `_compact_entry_rows` line 201) treats string factor labels verbatim via `normalise_rating_key` (str keys are deliberately verbatim, _rating.py:343), while `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key` (line 61, used by `_expand_entries_map.walk` line 225) migrates int-like float-strings ('5.'/'25.0'/'1e1' -> '5'/'25'/'10'). Preferred fix: route string factor keys on the WRITE side through the same int-like float-string migration as the read side, so a colliding pair is detected and `_insert_entry_value` raises `duplicate ... key` at SAVE time (fail-loud, per CLAUDE.md "no silent fallbacks") instead of producing an un-loadable sidecar. This also stops the silent single-label rewrite ('25.0'->'25' on load) by canonicalising both sides identically. Add a regression test asserting that compacting two entries with labels differing only in float-string formatting either raises on write or round-trips to the same canonical key (never write-OK-then-load-fail). Wave/branch context: this is on wave-2-cache-integrity touching the sidecar persistence path (_config_io.py save line 163 / load line 120).

real.description: When the main pipeline file directly connects an OUTPUT child node of one submodel to an INPUT child node of another submodel (e.g. `pipeline.connect("a_out", "b_in")` where a_out is a child of submodel A and b_in is a child of submodel B), merge_submodels produces a corrupt boundary edge. Submodel B's pass then sees tgt_inside and rebuilds a FRESH GraphEdge with target=submodel__B and targetHandle='in__b_in' but does NOT copy the existing sourceHandle, so the result is `submodel__A -> submodel__B` with targetHandle='in__b_in' and sourceHandle=None. Two downstream failures result, neither caught at parse time: (a) flatten=True path — flatten_graph (src/haute/_flatten.py:63-78) only rewrites the source side when sourceHandle is truthy; with sourceHandle=None the source stays 'submodel__A', the edge still references a submodel node at line 77, and the edge is dropped entirely, so the executor runs with the a_out→b_in data dependency silently removed (wrong execution order / missing data flow). (b) flatten=False (GUI/hierarchical) path — codegen later requires every edge whose source is a submodel placeholder to carry an 'out__<child>' sourceHandle and raises ParseError otherwise (codegen.py:1050-1057), so saving the parsed pipeline throws and the round-trip is broken. validate_pipeline_graph_shape_contracts does not detect it: _iter_submodel_child_contexts (src/haute/_graph_shape.py:115-118) computes `_boundary_child_id(None, prefix='out__')` → None and silently skips, so parse appears to succeed. (handle=None, source=submodel__A, target=submodel__B)". Root cause confirmed at _submodel_graph.py:116-125 (target-side branch builds a fresh GraphEdge with no sourceHandle arg) and :126-135 (source-side branch builds a fresh GraphEdge with no targetHandle arg) — whichever rewire_edges pass runs second discards the handle the first installed. flatten drop confirmed at _flatten.py:63 (source rewrite gated on truthy sh) -> :77 continue. This makes the edge-to-edge composition of the two passes commutative and yields submodel__A -> submodel__B with BOTH sh=out__a_out and th=in__b_in, which flatten_graph rewrites correctly to a_out -> b_in and which codegen accepts. Net effect: the semaphore permit count is incremented by one each time this race fires, silently and permanently raising the per-key concurrency cap (e.g. `_preview_work_slots` / `_trace_work_slots`), defeating the bounded-worker guarantee the coordinator exists to enforce. To still cover the genuine post-except cancellation-race where the acquire completed True after entering the handler, set holds_permit=True from the drained result ONLY when no prior release occurred in the body (i.e. the body did not already release). real.title: Textual [project] detection diverges from tomllib: quoted/dotted/array-of-tables project tables are missed, so a duplicate [project] is appended and `haute init` crashes
real.description: `_scan_table_headers` only recognises a literal bare `[project]` header. It returns the raw bracket text, so a quoted header `["project"]` yields header name '"project"' (with quotes) and a dotted-key table `project.dependencies = [...]` yields NO header at all. tomllib, however, treats all of these as a `project` table. `_find_project_table_bounds` compares `name == "project"` (exact, unquoted) and therefore returns None for these structurally-valid project tables. `_rewrite_project_dependencies` then takes its `bounds is None` branch (line 241-244) and APPENDS a fresh `[project]\ndependencies = [...]`, producing a file with TWO `project` declarations. tomllib rejects this with `Cannot declare ('project',) twice`, which is raised uncaught from `_ensure_haute_dependency` line 312. Net effect: running `haute init` in a directory whose existing pyproject.toml uses a quoted `["project"]` header or dotted `project.x = ...` keys crashes the command with a raw TOMLDecodeError and exit code 1.
real.evidence: Isolated repro (review/04-exhaustive/repro/V001.py, EXIT=0) and full CLI-boundary repro both confirm the predicted wrong behaviour. quoted-header `["project"]`: _scan_table_headers -> [(0,12,'"project"')]; _find_project_table_bounds -> None; _ensure_haute_dependency -> TOMLDecodeError: Cannot declare ('project',) twice (at line 6, column 9). dotted-keys `project.dependencies=[...]`: _scan_table_headers -> []; bounds -> None; same TOMLDecodeError (line 5). CliRunner(init,[]) on a quoted-header pyproject -> exit_code=1, exc=TOMLDecodeError("Cannot declare ('project',) twice ..."). _rewrite_project_dependencies output contains two `[project]` declarations (project count==2). For both inputs tomllib.loads(text)['project']['dependencies']==['polars'], proving these ARE valid project tables that the textual scanner misses.
real.fix: Stop deriving the [project] table location from the brittle textual scanner for the append/insert decision. Two robust options: (1) In _find_project_table_bounds, normalise each scanned header before comparison by parsing the bracket content as TOML key-syntax (strip surrounding quotes / take the first dotted segment) so '"project"' and the absence of a header for dotted keys are handled — but dotted keys still emit no header, so this alone is insufficient. (2) Preferred: make the rewrite authoritative via the already-parsed tomllib data. Since _ensure_haute_dependency already calls tomllib.loads(text) and knows whether parsed.get('project') exists, pass that fact in and only take the append-fresh-[project] branch when 'project' is genuinely absent from the parsed document; when 'project' exists but the textual scanner cannot locate a bare [project] header (quoted/dotted/array forms), fall back to a structural rewrite (e.g. rebuild with tomli-w or insert dependencies under the existing dotted/quoted form) instead of appending a duplicate table. Add regression tests covering ["project"] quoted headers, dotted project.* keys, and ensure no duplicate [project] is ever produced; also consider wrapping handle_init's TOMLDecodeError into a clean click error message as _serve.py already does.

real.title: `dependencies` key indented inside [project] is not matched, so a duplicate `dependencies` key is inserted, corrupting the file
real.description:

real.title: CLI pipeline_file override clobbers the resolved path, breaking directory-discovery in the no-toml deploy path
real.description: In the no-haute.toml branch, handle_deploy correctly resolves the user-supplied pipeline argument through resolve_pipeline_file (which accepts a directory and discovers the project pipeline inside it, returning an absolute file path) and feeds that resolved path into DeployConfig.from_cli_args. For a regular file argument the effect is merely cosmetic (the unresolved relative path still reads from cwd), but when the argument is a DIRECTORY (a documented, supported form per resolve_pipeline_file: '`haute run ./rating` is symmetric with `cd rating && haute run`'), the override replaces the discovered file with the directory itself. resolve_config then calls parse_pipeline_file(<directory>) -> read_user_text(<directory>) -> Path.read_text() which raises IsADirectoryError/PermissionError, caught by the broad `except Exception` at line 133 and surfaced as a confusing 'Resolution failed: [Is a directory]' SystemExit. So `haute deploy ./somedir` (no toml) is broken even though the equivalent `haute run ./somedir` / `haute lint ./somedir` work, because _run.py/_lint.py correctly use the `resolved` value (e.g. RunConfig(pipeline_file=resolved)) and never re-wrap the raw arg. Code trace confirms each step: _deploy.py:93-99 resolves the dir to a file via resolve_pipeline_file (_project.py:286-287 is_dir->_resolve_default_in) and feeds it to from_cli_args; _deploy.py:118-119 then sets overrides["pipeline_file"]=Path(config.pipeline_file) using the RAW './somedir' string; override() (_config.py:429 `val is not None and hasattr` -> setattr) writes the directory back; resolve_config (_config.py:543) -> parse_pipeline_file (parser.py:91) -> read_user_text (_io.py:461) Path(<dir>).read_text() raises (IsADirectoryError on POSIX / PermissionError on Windows), caught by the broad except at _deploy.py:133. By contrast _run.py:99 (RunConfig(pipeline_file=resolved)) and _lint.py:106 (LintConfig(pipeline_file=resolved)) use the resolved value and never re-wrap the raw arg, so `haute run ./dir` / `haute lint ./dir` work. In the no-haute.toml branch, from_cli_args already receives the resolved absolute file, so the raw-arg override is redundant and harmful: either (a) move the `if config.pipeline_file: overrides["pipeline_file"] = ...` line into the toml branch only (where `resolved` does not exist and the override legitimately overrides the TOML default), or (b) in the no-toml branch use the resolved path — `overrides["pipeline_file"] = resolved` — instead of `Path(config.pipeline_file)`. Several of these are row-preserving when used inside with_columns (e.g. df.with_columns(pl.sum('a').alias('s')) broadcasts the column sum across all rows and is a valid single-parent shape), so they legitimately reach the demand walks. The with_columns ordered guard at line 1145 does NOT bail because the expression is aliased (_alias_name is not None). The minimal fix, matching the module's existing "bail to full width on anything unprovable" invariant (the dynamic `pl.col(...)` branch at :796-801 already returns None), is to also return None whenever a `pl.<func>(...)` call with a string/non-`pl.col` argument cannot be proven column-free — so such nodes keep the safe full-width boundary instead of silently dropping the referenced column. A more precise (but more involved) alternative is to recognise the string argument of the known shortcuts (sum/mean/min/max/first/last/std/var/median/count/n_unique/...) as a column reference and add it to the set; this must enumerate only functions whose leading string arg names a column. real.title: Expression renderer drops required parentheses around Compare/BoolOp/IfExp/UnaryOp operands and around equal-precedence right-Pow, so the human-readable formula re-parses to a DIFFERENT value
real.description: _binop only adds parentheses when a child is itself an ast.BinOp (lines 223 and 225 both guard on `isinstance(node.left/right, ast.BinOp)`), and uses strict `<` precedence. This produces formulas that, when read by a human or re-parsed, compute a different number than the original Polars expression. Confirmed manifestations: (1) Compare operand inside arithmetic: `(pl.col('a') > pl.col('b')) + 1` renders as `a > b + 1`, which re-parses as `a > (b + 1)` (a boolean vs an arithmetic compare). (2) Unary-minus as power base: `(-pl.col('a')) ** 2` renders as `-a ** 2`, which Python parses as `-(a**2)` (sign flips for even powers). (3) Right-associative `**`: `(pl.col('a') ** pl.col('b')) ** pl.col('c')` renders as `a ** b ** c`, which re-parses as `a ** (b ** c)` (because the left-paren rule uses `<`, not `<=`, for the right-associative Pow). (4) IfExp operand: `(a if c else b) + 1` renders as `a if c else b + 1` -> reparses as `a if c else (b + 1)`. (5) BoolOp precedence in _boolop: `(a or b) and c` renders as `a or b and c`, which reparses as `a or (b and c)` because _boolop never wraps a lower-precedence `or` child inside an `and`. The rendered `expression_text` (and the parallel substituted_text) is written into user-facing trace lineage (`step.calculation`/`source_info`, per catalog finding 38), so the actuary is shown a formula that does not match the actual computation. This is the project's explicit fail-loud-vs-silent-wrong concern: a confidently-wrong formula with no error.

Each rendered string matches the predicted buggy output AND re-parses (standard Python) to a numerically different value than the source: (a > b) + 1 renders 'a > b + 1' -> source=2 vs reparse=True; (-a) ** 2 renders '-a ** 2' -> source=9 vs reparse=-9; (a ** b) ** c renders 'a ** b ** c' -> source=64 vs reparse=512; (a if c else b) + 1 renders 'a if c else b + 1' -> source=101 vs reparse=100; (a or b) and c renders 'a or b and c' -> source=0 vs reparse=1. Code-trace root cause confirmed in src/haute/_expression_parser.py: convert() (lines 152-186) dispatches operands by node type with no wrapping; _binop (214-234) only parenthesizes ast.BinOp children (lines 223/225) so Compare/BoolOp/UnaryOp/IfExp children are never wrapped, and line 223 uses strict '<' so an equal-precedence right-associative left-Pow is left unparenthesized; _boolop (257-260) joins values with no precedence awareness so an 'or' child inside 'and' loses its parens.

In _boolop, wrap any 'or'-valued child when emitting an 'and' (and generally wrap a lower-precedence BoolOp child). Add round-trip tests for: Compare-in-BinOp, unary-minus power base, (a**b)**c associativity, IfExp-in-BinOp, and or/and mixing, asserting the rendered text re-parses (ast) to the same operator grouping as the source. The computed result_value is unaffected (it uses _ExprEvaluator on the original AST), so this is a display/lineage-fidelity fix, but expression_text is surfaced verbatim to actuaries via _trace_export.py:36-44 (formula['expression']) and is itself re-parsed by _trace_waterfall.py:369-382 to label add-vs-multiply, so the wrong grouping is both shown to users and consumed internally.

real.title: ast.walk BFS ordering breaks 'last match wins' for chained .with_columns(...).with_columns(...) that redefine the same column, selecting the shadowed (overwritten) definition
real.description: _find_with_columns_calls collects with_columns/select calls via ast.walk(tree). ast.walk is breadth-first, so for a single chained expression df.with_columns(A).with_columns(B) the OUTER call (B, which Polars applies LAST and which therefore wins) is yielded BEFORE the inner call (A). parse_expression (and _compute_result_impl and _evaluate_conditional_branches) iterate wc_calls and keep the LAST alias match ('last match wins', comment at line 1078). Because walk order is reverse-of-execution for chained calls, the loop's 'last' is actually the inner/earliest (shadowed) definition A, not the effective definition B. The displayed formula, expression_type, referenced_columns AND the computed result_value all reflect the overwritten definition. No exception is raised, so the broad except-catch-all (known finding #23) is NOT involved — this is a confidently-wrong value/formula. Note the equivalent code written as two SEPARATE statements works correctly, because there the two Assign/Call nodes are siblings at the same depth and ast.walk preserves their source order; only the chained form is wrong.
real.evidence: Repro output (uv run, Polars 1.39.2): "[oracle] Polars effective value of 'out' = 110"; "[walk] _find_with_columns_calls order (BFS) = ['+100', '+1']"; "[chained] parse_expression.expression_text = 'a + 1'"; "[chained] evaluate_expression.result_value = 11"; "[chained] substituted_text = '10 + 1'"; control "[control] result_value = 110 ('a + 100')". For df.with_columns(A).with_columns(B), the outer Call B is the PARENT of inner Call A (B.func.value IS A), so ast.walk (BFS) yields B before A. _find_with_columns_calls (_expression_parser.py:914-922) returns that walk order; the "last match wins" loop at :1081-1086 (also :1562-1566 in _compute_result_impl and :1466-1471 in _evaluate_conditional_branches, and the col_defs dict-overwrite at :2199-2201) therefore keeps the SHADOWED inner def A (+1) instead of the effective outer def B (+100). All asserts pass: chained result_value==11 (!=Polars 110), expression_text=='a + 1' (no '100'), while the separate-statement control correctly yields 'a + 100'/110 — isolating the chained form + BFS ordering as the cause. Grep of the whole file confirms NO reversed()/source-order sort/de-dup guards wc_calls anywhere; the plain chained form is not intercepted by the control-flow/opaque guards (it returns a concrete wrong value, not opaque).
real.fix: Make _find_with_columns_calls return calls in EXECUTION order rather than ast.walk BFS order so the "last match wins" consumers select the effective (outermost-applied) definition. Two robust options: (a) sort the collected (call, lineno) results so that, among nodes sharing the same source span start, the one with the larger end_col_offset/end_lineno (the OUTER chained call, executed last) comes LAST — i.e. sort by (lineno, col_offset, end_lineno, end_col_offset) ascending; in the chained case the inner call (end_col=57) then precedes the outer (end_col=109), and separate statements remain in source order. (b) Equivalently, detect chained calls structurally (outer.func.value is the inner Call) and emit the inner before the outer. Apply the same ordering to the col_defs overwrite at :2186-2201. Add regression tests covering chained .with_columns(A).with_columns(B) redefining one alias (assert effective B wins for expression_text, result_value, substituted_text) plus the separate-statement equivalent and a 3-deep chain, so future ordering regressions are caught. Per CLAUDE.md TDD: write the failing test first (the repro at review/04-exhaustive/repro/V009.py demonstrates the expected/actual values to encode).

real.title: Outer .otherwise() containing a nested when corrupts outer branch metadata (reports wrong taken_branch/index/dimmed)
real.description: In _BranchTrackingEvaluator._eval_clauses, the `then` path sets `self._is_outer = False` (line 2094) before recursing into the then value, but the `otherwise` path (lines 2107-2113) sets taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches WITHOUT clearing `self._is_outer`. So when the outer `.otherwise()` value itself contains a nested when-chain, `self.evaluate(clause['otherwise'])` (line 2113) recurses into the inner chain's _eval_clauses with `is_outer = self._is_outer` still True. The inner chain then overwrites taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches with ITS OWN (inner) values, clobbering the outer's. The trace therefore reports that the outer THEN clause fired when in fact the outer OTHERWISE fired. This metadata is serialized verbatim into step.calculation via dataclasses.asdict(evaluated) (_trace_enrichment.py:1523) and drives which clause the explainability UI highlights/dims, so the user is shown the wrong branch as taken.
real.evidence: Case A: code=pl.when(a>0).then(99).otherwise(pl.when(b>0).then(1).otherwise(2)), row a=-1,b=1. evaluate_expression returns result_value=1 (correct: value can ONLY come from outer-otherwise -> inner-then; outer-then would be 99), yet taken_branch='then', taken_branch_index=0, dimmed_branches=[1] -- i.e. it reports the OUTER THEN (index 0) as taken when the OUTER OTHERWISE (index 1) actually fired. Control Case B (nesting under outer THEN, row a=1,b=1) is reported correctly (taken_branch='then', index 0, nested_branches=['then']), isolating the missing `_is_outer=False` on the otherwise path as the root cause. Code-trace of consumer chain: evaluate_expression (_expression_parser.py:1393-1398, 1411-1414) -> _evaluate_conditional_branches (1476-1483) -> _trace_enrichment.py:1523-1528 serializes taken_branch/taken_branch_index into step.calculation, which drives UI highlight/dim.
real.fix: In _BranchTrackingEvaluator._eval_clauses (src/haute/_expression_parser.py ~2107-2113), make the otherwise path mirror the then path: when `is_outer`, after recording taken_branch='otherwise'/index/dimmed, set `self._is_outer = False` before `self.evaluate(clause['otherwise'])`. Then, mirroring the then-path post-recursion restore (lines 2098-2104), if the otherwise value contains a nested when (`self._check_nested_when(clause['otherwise'])`), capture the nested chain's branch into `self.nested_branches` and re-assert the outer otherwise metadata (taken_branch='otherwise', taken_branch_index=otherwise_idx, dimmed_branches=[j for j!=otherwise_idx]) after the recursive evaluate returns, so the nested values do not clobber the outer ones. Add a regression test for an outer .otherwise() wrapping a when-chain asserting taken_branch='otherwise'.

real.title: Banding column contract declares produced output even when the factor has no rules (runtime skips it)
real.description: _banding_columns reports a factor's outputColumn as a produced column whenever both 'column' and 'outputColumn' are non-empty: `produced = {f["outputColumn"] for f in factors if f.get("outputColumn")}`. But the runtime _apply_banding_factors skips any factor whose rules are empty: `if not col or not out or not rules: continue`. The projection demand-propagation subtracts produced columns from upstream demand (projection.py:2321 `base_contribution = (my_needed - produced) | referenced`), so if a downstream node demands that outputColumn, the demand is removed at the banding node (contract claims ownership) but no column is materialised -> downstream select/reference fails with column-not-found in projected/bounded profiles. [A] get_column_contract(NodeType.BANDING, {factors:[{column:age, outputColumn:age_band}]}) -> produced=['age_band'], referenced=['age'] (no rules check). [B] _apply_banding_factors(LazyFrame{age}, [ruleless]).collect().columns == ['age'] (age_band NOT created); contrast [B'] same factor + 1 rule -> ['age','age_band']. Preferably normalise first to match exactly what the executor sees: `factors = _normalise_banding_factors(config); produced = {f["outputColumn"] for f in factors if f.get("column") and f.get("outputColumn") and (f.get("rules") or [])}; referenced = {f["column"] for f in factors if f.get("column")}`. real.title: _cached_output_names raises AttributeError on multi-port apiInput parents (dict output has no .columns)
real.description: _cached_output_names is the schema-warning helper used when an instance node (config['instanceOf']) is present: it sums the columns feeding the instance and the original by calling _cached_output_names(pid) for each parent. For a multi-port apiInput source, _execute_eager_core stores output_columns[nid] = [] and available_columns[nid] = [] (an EMPTY list, not absent) while eager_outputs[nid] is a dict[port_label, DataFrame] (src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1900-1904). This loop runs inside execute_graph's try/finally that only manages the cache pin — it is NOT covered by the per-node error swallowing of _eager_execute(swallow_errors=True) — so the exception propagates out of execute_graph and fails the entire preview/trace request (HTTP 500) rather than degrading one node. Trigger: a multi-port apiInput wired as a direct parent of any node carrying instanceOf (or of the referenced original). Multi-port apiInput sources and instance nodes are both shipped features and nothing structurally forbids wiring them together.
real.evidence: Repro output: `AttributeError("'dict' object has no attribute 'columns'")` raised OUT OF execute_graph. Traceback tail: executor.py:1120 `inst_input_cols.update(_cached_output_names(pid))` -> executor.py:1107 `return set(df.columns) if df is not None else set()` -> AttributeError. `via _cached_output_names: True`, `AttributeError on .columns: True`. The exception was caught only by the outer harness except (not by any per-node swallow), proving it escapes execute_graph entirely and would fail the whole preview/trace request (HTTP 500). The unrelated `node_failed`/"No input data available for node 'orig'" log is a swallowed per-node error and does NOT cause the crash — the warning loop crashes regardless on the multi-port `api` parent of the instance node.
real.fix: In `_cached_output_names` (executor.py:1102-1107), make it multi-port-aware exactly as the per-node results loop already does at executor.py:1182-1184. After `df = eager_outputs.get(node_id)`, handle the dict case: `if isinstance(df, dict): return set().union(*(set(f.columns) for f in df.values()))` (union of all ports' columns — consistent with the union-across-parents semantics the schema-warning loop already uses). Then keep `return set(df.columns) if df is not None else set()` for the single-frame/None case. Add a regression test: a multi-port apiInput wired as a direct parent of an instanceOf node (and separately, of the referenced original) must let execute_graph return per-node NodeResults instead of raising. The existing harness in tests/test_apiinput_multi_port_runtime.py (`_multi_port_config`, `_build_cache_for`, isolated_root fixture) plus a node carrying `config={"instanceOf": ...}` provides the full setup. Optionally, prefer per-port columns via avail_cols/column_cache keyed by (node_id, port_label) for a more precise warning, but the dict-aware union is the minimal correct fix.

real.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1203/1213 (infer_v2_schema_from_data builds column path `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with an unescaped key) consumed by _resolve_leaf dotted-walk at :526-536
real.title: infer_v2_schema_from_data manufactures a dotted column path for a JSON key that literally contains a dot, so the shred silently resolves the value to None (value lost, not even counted as a skip)
real.description: Inference emits an object column whose path is `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with no escaping of `col_name`. For a record with a key that itself contains a dot (e.g. `"a.b": 42`), this yields column path `$[*].a.b`, and `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `a.b`. The dotted leaf is then interpreted by `_resolve_leaf` (lines 526-536) as a NESTED path: it walks `value.get("a")` then `.get("b")`, which is absent (the real key is the single string `"a.b"`), so the column resolves to None. The original value is silently lost and the row is still emitted with None (so it is not surfaced by skip accounting either). The schema also round-trips through validate_v2_schema cleanly, hiding the problem. This shares the `_resolve_leaf` dotted-ambiguity root with catalogued finding #12/BUG-N3 (a list at an intermediate dotted segment), but the NEW angle is that inference itself fabricates these ambiguous flat-key-as-dotted-path columns with no guard, making it reachable from the ordinary Infer Tables -> Cache as Parquet flow rather than only from hand-authored configs.
real.evidence: Repro output: inferred column paths {'a.b': '$[*].a.b', 'ok': '$[*].ok'}; shredded rows [{'a.b': None, 'ok': 1}]; skip total 0. Source value 42 under flat key 'a.b' was silently dropped to None while sibling 'ok'=1 survived and no skip was counted. Code-trace: infer (_json_shred.py:1213-1214) emits path f"{table_path}.{col_name}" with no escaping -> parse_column_path("$[*].a.b","$[*]") (_api_input_schema.py:224-255) returns leaf "a.b" -> shred (_json_shred.py:634-639) calls _resolve_leaf({'a.b':42},'a.b') (lines 526-536): '.' in leaf -> value.get('a')=None -> returns None. Row still emitted (object dict matches object table at line 630, is_scalar_table=False==not is_dict=False), so no row-skip. validate_v2_schema (_api_input_schema.py:293-403) has B1/B2/B3 guards but NONE rejecting a dotted/ambiguous column name, so the schema round-trips cleanly. infer_v2_schema_from_data is reachable from the ordinary cache flow (routes/json_cache.py:534).
real.fix: The root ambiguity is that a leaf string serves double duty as both a flat key and a dotted nested-path. Two complementary defenses: (1) Detect-and-fail at validate time — when parse_column_path yields a leaf containing '.', this is only legitimate if a corresponding intermediate object table/path exists; otherwise (and definitely for inferred flat keys) raise ApiInputSchemaError naming the offending column, so the loss is loud rather than silent (matches the codebase's fail-loud philosophy and the existing B1/B2/B3 guard pattern). (2) Preferred long-term: introduce an escaping convention for path segments (e.g. backslash-escape '.' in a key) and apply it in infer_v2_schema_from_data when building f"{table_path}.{col_name}" AND in parse_column_path / _resolve_leaf when splitting, so literal-dot keys round-trip losslessly. At minimum, infer_v2_schema_from_data must not silently manufacture an ambiguous path for a key containing '.'; either escape it or raise. Add a regression test covering a top-level key like "a.b" through the full Infer -> shred flow asserting the value survives (or that validation rejects it loudly), per CLAUDE.md's failing-test-first rule.

real.title: Fast-path cache key drops `version` while the canonical key keeps it, so run-sourced catboost/rustystats models load from disk twice and leave a permanently-orphaned duplicate cache entry (and skewed hit/miss counters); pyfunc loses the fast path entirely
real.description: load_mlflow_model has two cache-key construction sites that disagree for `source_type="run"` whenever a non-empty `version` is supplied. The fast-path (lines 893-900) hardcodes `version=""`, so `_model_cache_key` (lines 311-313: truthy version -> 5-tuple, else 4-tuple) returns the 4-tuple `("run", run_id, artifact_path, task)`. The slow-path (lines 968-974) passes `version=resolved_version`, and for a run source `resolve_mlflow_source` returns `resolved_version = version` unchanged (_mlflow_utils.py:101,109-111). Production callers ALWAYS pass `version=config.get("version", "latest")` even for run sources (src/haute/_builders.py:1196; src/haute/_model_explainability.py:569; threaded through ModelScorer._load_scoring_model_uncached at _model_scorer.py:1063-1070). With `version="latest"` (truthy) the slow-path stores the model under the 5-tuple `("run", run_id, "latest", artifact_path, task)` while the fast-path only ever looks up / stores the 4-tuple. The two keys can never coincide. real.title: canonical_json is NON-deterministic for sets/frozensets containing NaN floats — violates the documented order-independence contract for unordered containers
real.description: canonical_json's contract (module docstring lines 81-99 and _canonicalise docstring lines 119-123) promises that sets/frozensets 'whose elements are the same regardless of the order they were inserted' encode identically because unordered containers are sorted. This is broken when a set/frozenset contains two or more NaN floats. _canonicalise (line 141-143) calls sorted(members, key=_sort_key); _sort_key maps every float (NaN included) to ('2_num', value). Because all NaN comparisons return False, sorted() cannot impose a total order on the NaN members and leaves them in their incoming (hash-/insertion-determined, hence arbitrary) relative positions. Distinct NaN objects also have distinct, effectively-arbitrary hashes, so the set's iteration order — and therefore which slots the surrounding non-NaN elements occupy relative to the NaN run — varies. Result: two logically-equal sets produce DIFFERENT canonical JSON, so two identical configs/policies yield different fingerprints (phantom cache misses), and the digest is unstable across processes/insertion orders. This is silent: sorted() does not raise, so the 'fail loud, never silent' guarantee the surrounding code advertises is bypassed for this case. The property test deliberately excludes NaN (tests/test_caching_correctness.py:504-510 uses allow_nan=False with a comment that NaN breaks equality), confirming the case is unhandled rather than intentionally specified. canonical_json is THE digest encoder (used by _graph_base_fingerprint node configs, runtime_input_extra_keys, and _dataframe_execution_cache execution_policy/payload, the last of which the code comments explicitly note may contain sets).
real.evidence: Repro (EXIT=0, deterministic asserts) proves the mechanism and contract violation. Part 1 — sorted() is a NO-OP for NaN: sorted([nan,1.0,nan,2.0,nan,3.0], key=_sort_key) = ['NaN',1.0,'NaN',2.0,'NaN',3.0] but sorted([1.0,nan,2.0,nan,3.0,nan], key=_sort_key) = [1.0,'NaN',2.0,'NaN',3.0,'NaN'] (same multiset, different output). Part 2 — the EXACT internal pipeline canonical_json(sorted(members,key=_sort_key)) yields '[NaN,1.0,NaN,2.0,NaN,3.0]' vs '[1.0,NaN,2.0,NaN,3.0,NaN]' for two legitimate set-iteration orders of the logically-equal set. Corroboration: one unseeded process produced 10 distinct encodings for {NaN,NaN,NaN,1.0,2.0,3.0}; 6 separate interpreter runs each produced 4 distinct outputs. Control: list path = 1 output (stable), isolating the defect to the set/frozenset sort path. _sort_key(NaN)==('2_num', nan); all '<' comparisons vs nan return False so Timsort leaves NaN in incoming (set-iteration, hash/insertion-determined) order.
real.fix: Make non-finite floats order deterministically AND identically among themselves in src/haute/_cache.py:_sort_key. In the int/float branch, detect math.isnan(value) (and math.isinf) and return a stable secondary key that (a) is byte-identical for every NaN so a set canonicalises to a fixed NaN-run rather than an arbitrary interleaving, and (b) keeps a total order against finite numbers (e.g. sort NaN after all finite values: return ("2_num_nan", 0) for NaN, and for finite floats keep ("2_num", value)). Because canonical values are JSON-safe and finite numbers compare fine, only the NaN/inf cases need special handling. Then extend the property test (tests/test_caching_correctness.py around the _canonical_scalars block at 503-512) to include sets/frozensets containing multiple NaN and assert canonical_json is invariant across shuffled-insertion copies. Do NOT swallow this with a fallback — the encoder must remain deterministic and loud for genuinely unsupported types.

The same non-injective pattern recurs in graph_fingerprint (line 431): combined = "\n".join([*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]) — an extra_key containing a newline collides with a different extra_keys tuple. The module deliberately framed EDGES with canonical_json arrays specifically to be collision-proof (see the lines 205-217 comment: 'quoting/escaping rules out separator-content collisions'), but the NODE line and the graph_fingerprint join were left in the unframed delimiter form — an internal inconsistency. Consequence: cache cross-contamination — preview/trace/dataframe-execution entries for one graph (or one set of execution params) served as fresh for a genuinely different one. This is DISTINCT from the known duplicate-node-id finding (findings.json:906, which is about node_map collapsing two same-id nodes); here the colliding ids/keys are different strings and the collision is in the digest material itself.

real.fix: Make the node-line and the graph_fingerprint join injective by framing them with canonical_json, exactly as edges already are. In _graph_base_fingerprint (src/haute/_cache.py:199-201) replace the f-string node line with canonical_json([n.id, str(n.data.nodeType), _node_config_for_execution_fingerprint(n)]); the existing sort key (n.id) stays valid. In graph_fingerprint (src/haute/_cache.py:429-432) replace combined = "\n".join([*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]) with a framed encoding, e.g. combined = canonical_json([list(extra_keys), context_parts, base]); since this changes digest bytes, bump ALGO_VERSION (5 -> 6) and update the version-history comment so previously-cached entries are invalidated rather than colliding across the format change. Add regression tests asserting: (a) the 1-node-vs-2-node crafted-id graphs now produce DIFFERENT base fingerprints, and (b) graph_fingerprint(g,'k1\nk2') != graph_fingerprint(g,'k1','k2'). This also removes the bespoke f-string format, unifying with the edge handling.

real.title: Large worker results deadlock: parent joins the child before draining the result queue (classic mp.Queue feeder-pipe deadlock)
real.description: run_isolated_worker fully waits for the child to exit (_wait_for_worker loops on process.join until not process.is_alive()) BEFORE it ever reads the result queue (_read_worker_payload -> result_queue.get). With multiprocessing.Queue, the child's put() hands the serialized object to a background feeder thread that writes it into an OS pipe with a finite buffer (~64 KiB on Linux). If the pickled result exceeds the pipe buffer, the feeder blocks on the pipe write until the parent reads. But the parent never reads during the wait phase; it only join()s. At interpreter shutdown the child blocks in Queue._finalize_join waiting for the feeder, so the child never exits, and the parent's join() never returns. This is the exact deadlock documented in the stdlib ('a process that has put items in a queue will wait before terminating until all the buffered items are fed... if you join such a process you may get a deadlock'). The module never calls cancel_join_thread and never drains the queue before joining, so the pattern is unconditional.
real.evidence: review/04-exhaustive/repro/V036.py output: "completed_within_watchdog: False / elapsed_seconds: 30.02 / returned_len: None" for a 16 MiB result whose worker allocates-and-returns instantly (process then killed by outer timeout, EXIT 124). Control bracketing in a second run: 1 KiB -> completed=True returned_len=1024 (fast, correct value); 32 KiB / 128 KiB / 1 MiB -> completed=False (wedged at 12s watchdog) -- deadlock is threshold-driven by payload crossing the OS pipe buffer, not an import/setup error. Code trace (_worker_isolation.py): line 194 result_queue=ctx.Queue(maxsize=1) with no cancel_join_thread; line 211 _wait_for_worker runs FIRST and lines 329-344 loop `while process.is_alive(): process.join(timeout=...)` never calling result_queue.get; line 213 _read_worker_payload->result_queue.get(timeout=1.0) reached only AFTER the loop; child line 270 result_queue.put(("ok", fn(...))) then returns -> feeder blocks on full pipe -> child shutdown finalizer joins feeder -> child never exits -> is_alive() stays True -> with default timeout_seconds=None parent loops forever. Existing test_isolated_worker_returns_picklable_value passes (2.31s), confirming the primitive works only for tiny results.
real.fix: Drain the result queue concurrently with waiting instead of join-before-drain. In _wait_for_worker, attempt a short-timeout/non-blocking result_queue.get inside the poll loop and stash the payload (so the child's feeder thread can flush and the child can exit), then have _read_worker_payload consume the stashed payload; alternatively have the child call result_queue.cancel_join_thread() so it can exit without the parent draining first. Add a TDD regression test that returns a multi-MiB payload under a bounded timeout and asserts the exact bytes round-trip (it currently hangs). Keep terminate/timeout/stop-reason paths unchanged.

real.title: Verbatim string factor labels that look like int-like floats are silently corrupted on compact->expand round trip
real.description: The compact-write side (`_compact_entry_rows` -> `_canonical_sidecar_key` -> `normalise_rating_key`) keeps string factor labels VERBATIM (strings are never collapsed by `normalise_rating_key`). But the expand-read side (`_expand_entries_map.walk` -> `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`) applies a 'legacy float-string migration' that collapses any int-like float-string map key: '25.0'->'25', '1.0'->'1', '1e1'->'10', '5.'->'5'. So a legitimate, non-numeric string label such as a price band '25.0' (or any banding/categorical label that happens to parse as an int-valued float) is silently rewritten after a single save/load cycle. The rating lookup join keys on the exact label, so after `collect_node_configs` (compact write) + `parse_pipeline_source` (expand read) the table entry's key changes and the row STOPS MATCHING -- a silent wrong-result defect, not an error. The `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key` docstring frames this as scoped legacy migration, but it cannot distinguish a legacy float that `str()` wrote as '25.0' from a genuine verbatim string label '25.0', and `normalise_rating_key`'s own docstring explicitly promises 'String keys are deliberately verbatim -- 25.0 is a label, not a number, and never collapses', which the expand path violates.
real.evidence: Executed repro output: `_canonical_sidecar_key('25.0') (WRITE) -> '25.0'` but `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key('25.0') (READ) -> '25'`. Full JSON round trip of a row-array entry: `rehydrated entries (1 factor): [{'band': '25', 'value': 7.0}]` (label changed from '25.0' to '25'). Engine consequence: pre-round-trip `f = [7.0]` (matches), post-round-trip raises `RatingTableMissError ... Missing key(s): {'band': '25.0'}`; with a neutral default the same defect is a SILENT wrong value `f = [-1.0]` instead of 7.0. 3-factor variant: `{'a': '1', 'b': 'North', 'c': 'online', ...}` (only the int-like float-string 'a' is corrupted). All asserts passed -> "V038 REPRODUCED".
real.fix: Make the expand-read side stop unconditionally collapsing int-like float-strings. The compact-WRITE side now canonicalises numeric factor values to their collapsed integer form (float 25.0 -> map key "25"), so a current sidecar can never legitimately contain a "25.0" key produced from a number — only a genuine verbatim string label or a TRUE legacy save can. Options, best first: (1) Drop the lossy migration in `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key` and keep compact map keys verbatim on read (mirror `normalise_rating_key`'s string-verbatim contract), accepting that pre-collapse legacy sidecars must be migrated by a one-shot offline pass rather than silently on every load; this restores write==read symmetry. (2) If legacy-key migration must remain, gate it behind an explicit per-table schema/version marker written by new saves (e.g. a sidecar `compactKeyVersion`) so the read side only migrates files that predate the collapse, and treats unmarked/new-version keys as verbatim. Either way, add a failing-then-passing test: round-trip a row-array entry `{"band": "25.0", "value": 7.0}` through `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar` + json dump/load + `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` and assert the label stays "25.0" (and that `apply_rating_step_from_config` on a string frame column ["25.0"] still returns 7.0). Pins the asymmetry against regression. Note the same migration also exists for nested factors and is covered by the 3-factor variant in the repro.

real.title: Chained and keyword-form pipeline.submodel(...) calls are silently dropped, discarding entire submodels
real.description: extract_submodel_calls only recognises the single, positional, non-chained form `pipeline.submodel("path")`. It requires the call's `func.value` to be a bare `ast.Name` equal to "pipeline" and reads only `call.args[0]`. Two valid, runtime-supported spellings are therefore silently ignored, returning an empty path list so every referenced submodel (and all of its nodes and edges) vanishes from the parsed graph with no warning: (1) the documented chained form `pipeline.submodel("a.py").submodel("b.py")`, and (2) the keyword form `pipeline.submodel(file="a.py")`. Chaining is explicitly documented in the runtime (`Pipeline.submodel` returns `self`, docstring at src/haute/pipeline.py:477 says "Can be chained: pipeline.submodel(\"a.py\").submodel(\"b.py\")") and is exercised by tests/test_pipeline.py:786 and :792. The sibling helper _extract_connect_calls (src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:336-381) walks method chains down to the base receiver and accepts positional-or-keyword source/target; extract_submodel_calls does neither, so the two paths disagree. Codegen always emits one `pipeline.submodel(\"...\")` per line (codegen.py:1241) so GUI round-trips are unaffected, but any hand-authored pipeline file that uses the documented chaining (or the keyword) syntax silently loses its submodels. This is a silent contract violation that drops graph content rather than failing loudly, contrary to the project's fail-loud policy.
real.evidence: Repro output: chained form `pipeline.submodel('modules/a.py').submodel('modules/b.py')` -> extract_submodel_calls returns [] (expected ['modules/a.py','modules/b.py']); keyword form `pipeline.submodel(file='modules/a.py')` -> returns [] (expected ['modules/a.py']); baseline one-per-line correctly returns both paths; `module.pipeline.submodel(...)` correctly stays []. Root cause traced: _parser_submodels.py:49-54 requires func.value to be a bare ast.Name=='pipeline' (chained outer call's func.value is itself an ast.Call -> isinstance(...,ast.Name) is False -> whole expr skipped), and line 55 reads only call.args[0] (keyword form has empty call.args -> guard False). Downstream impact confirmed: parser.py:182-184 gates submodel handling on `if submodel_paths and ...`; an empty list silently skips parsing+merging the submodel, so its nodes/edges vanish with no warning. Runtime contract is real: pipeline.py:480 `return self` (chainable), docstring pipeline.py:477, and tests/test_pipeline.py:786,792 assert chaining. Sibling _ast_helpers.py:364-373 (_extract_connect_calls) walks the chain to the base receiver and accepts positional-or-keyword, confirming the two parser paths disagree.
real.fix: Mirror _extract_connect_calls in extract_submodel_calls: walk the method chain from the outermost Call down to its base receiver, collecting every link whose func.attr == 'submodel'; require the terminal base `cur` to be a bare ast.Name with id == 'pipeline' (this preserves the existing test_parser_submodels.py:43-56 rejection of `module.pipeline.submodel(...)` and non-pipeline receivers). For each collected link, resolve the path from either call.args[0] (ast.Constant) or a `file=` keyword (ast.Constant), in source order (reverse the outermost-first link list). Add tests for the chained form, the keyword form, and a mixed chain, and re-assert that module.pipeline.submodel(...) and bare pipeline.submodel() (no path) remain rejected. Per the fail-loud policy, consider that this only matters for hand-authored files since codegen.py:1241 emits one call per line.

real.title: Positional-only and keyword-only @pipeline node parameters are silently dropped (only ast.arguments.args is read), losing implicit edges and corrupting user-code/config extraction
real.description: _extract_decorated_nodes builds param_names from `stmt.args.args` only. Python's ast.arguments splits parameters into posonlyargs (before `/`), args (positional-or-keyword), kwonlyargs (after `*`), vararg, and kwarg. Reading just `args` means a pipeline node written as `def node(a, /, b, *, claims_aggregate):` exposes only `b`. Every parameter that names an upstream node but lives in the posonly/kwonly buckets is invisible: its implicit param-name edge is never created by _build_edges, its input-extraction line is not recognised as boilerplate by extract_user_code (mis-extracting the saved code), and for LIVE_SWITCH/CONSTANT-style nodes it is missing from config['inputs']. No error is raised -- a silent contract violation in the same family as the known async-def and submodel-edge drops, but distinct from them and not covered by any known finding. (Machine-generated codegen never emits `/` or `*`, so this only bites hand-edited pipelines, but those are an explicitly supported edit surface.)
real.evidence: Repro output: "[A] EXPECTED implicit edge ('adjustments', 'transform') from kw-only param, but it is MISSING. edges=[('claims', 'transform')]" and "[B] EXPECTED implicit edge ('upstream', 'downstream') from positional-only param, but it is MISSING. edges=[('other', 'downstream')]" and "[C] codegen alias 'df = claims' leaked into config['code']... code='df = claims\ndf = df.filter(pl.col(\"x\") > 0)'". Root cause confirmed at src/haute/_graph_builders.py:73 `param_names = [arg.arg for arg in stmt.args.args]` (only the positional-or-keyword bucket; posonlyargs/kwonlyargs grepped nowhere in src/haute). Downstream _build_edges (line 144) and _finalise_polars alias-stripping both consume param_names.
real.fix: At src/haute/_graph_builders.py:73 flatten all keyword-bearing parameter buckets in source order rather than reading only `args`: `param_names = [a.arg for a in (*stmt.args.posonlyargs, *stmt.args.args, *stmt.args.kwonlyargs)]`. This single change fixes every downstream consumer (implicit-edge derivation in _build_edges, the n_params count, and the codegen-alias stripping in extract_user_code / the per-kind extractors). Deliberately exclude vararg/kwarg (*args/**kwargs): they cannot name a single upstream node under the per-name edge model and would create spurious edges. Add a parser test with a node like `def transform(claims, *, adjustments)` and `def node(upstream, /, other)` asserting the kw-only and positional-only implicit edges are present, plus a transform whose body opens `df = <posonly_param>` asserting the alias is stripped from config['code'].

real.title: rewire_edges silently drops the external endpoint's port handle on cross-boundary edges, corrupting multi-port wiring
real.description: When rewire_edges replaces a cross-boundary edge, it correctly synthesises the SUBMODEL-side boundary handle (in__<child> / out__<child>) but throws away the handle on the *external* side of the edge. In the External->internal branch it builds GraphEdge(source=e.source, target=sm_node_id, targetHandle=f'in__{e.target}') with no sourceHandle=e.sourceHandle, so an external multi-output source node feeding a submodel child loses its output-port selector. Symmetrically, the Internal->external branch sets sourceHandle=f'out__{e.source}' but omits targetHandle=e.targetHandle, dropping the external target's input-port role. The module's sibling reconstruction code in _parser_submodels.py:159-167 deliberately preserves these handles (sourceHandle=source_port, targetHandle=target_port) precisely so that 'later rewiring replaces true submodel boundary handles with in__/out__ markers' (comment at _parser_submodels.py:139-142) -- i.e. only the boundary side should be replaced, not the far side. The flatten round-trip (_flatten.py) only restores the target side, and ONLY for edge-join roles via build_edge_join_boundary_target_roles (_flatten.py:30-33, 74); there is NO recovery path for a dropped source-side handle (when a submodel is the SOURCE, _flatten.py:67 sets new_sh=None unconditionally). Consequently a graph that wires an external multi-output node (e.g. a model node emitting frequency/severity frames, or a multi-port apiInput) into a node inside a newly-created submodel ends up, after flatten-for-execution, with an edge from that multi-port node carrying sourceHandle=None, which _execute_lazy.py:103-108 rejects with ValueError 'Edge from multi-port node X has no sourceHandle'. Worse, in the hierarchical (flatten=False) saved graph the wiring intent is silently lost with no error at all. Both callers are affected: routes/_submodel_ops.py:90 passes real GraphEdge objects (cross_edges) straight from graph.edges with handles intact, and _parser_submodels.py:194 passes parent_edge_list whose cross edges carry the preserved source_port/target_port.
real.evidence: Repro output (exit 1): Part 1A External->internal: input sourceHandle='frequency' -> result sourceHandle=None (targetHandle correctly 'in__child'). Part 1B Internal->external: input targetHandle='base' -> result targetHandle=None (sourceHandle correctly 'out__child'). Part 2 after flatten_graph the ext->child edge has sourceHandle=None. Part 3 _pick_source_frame raises exactly: "ValueError: Edge from multi-port node 'ext' has no sourceHandle. Expected one of: ['frequency', 'severity']." Code confirms src/haute/_submodel_graph.py:123 only sets targetHandle=f"in__{e.target}" and :132 only sets sourceHandle=f"out__{e.source}"; e.sourceHandle/e.targetHandle on the external side are never referenced. _flatten.py:67 sets new_sh=None unconditionally for submodel-source edges, so no source-side recovery exists. _parser_submodels.py:159-167 builds cross edges WITH sourceHandle=source_port/targetHandle=target_port (preserving them), and routes/_submodel_ops.py:90 passes real GraphEdge cross_edges from graph.edges with handles intact — so both callers feed handle-bearing edges into the lossy rewire_edges. No guard rejects multi-port sources feeding a submodel.
real.fix: In src/haute/_submodel_graph.py rewire_edges, forward the far-side handle in both cross-boundary branches: in the External->internal branch add sourceHandle=e.sourceHandle (alongside targetHandle=f"in__{e.target}"); in the Internal->external branch add targetHandle=e.targetHandle (alongside sourceHandle=f"out__{e.source}"). Then in src/haute/_flatten.py:67, stop overwriting the source handle with None for submodel-source edges — keep the carried external source port (new_sh = edge.sourceHandle) so the flattened edge still names the multi-port. For the target side at _flatten.py:74, prefer the edge_join_boundary_target_roles role when present but fall back to the carried targetHandle (new_th = edge_join_boundary_target_roles.get((original_tgt, tgt, src), edge.targetHandle)) instead of clobbering it to None. Add TDD coverage: extend tests/test_submodel_graph.py TestRewireEdges with an inbound edge carrying sourceHandle and an outbound edge carrying targetHandle, asserting the far-side handle survives; and an end-to-end flatten test asserting a multi-port source -> submodel-child edge retains its source port after flatten so _pick_source_frame succeeds.

real.title: build_report reports post-truncation length as sampled_rows, breaking the sampled = scored + failed invariant
real.description: When staging and production prediction lists differ in length, build_report truncates input_df to `scored` (line 427) and then reports `sampled_rows=len(input_df)` (line 449) using the already-truncated length. However `failed` (line 422) is computed against the ORIGINAL input_df length. The result is a self-contradictory report where sampled_rows != scored_rows + failed_rows: the header line in format_terminal/format_markdown shows '(N of total sampled)' with the wrong (too-small) N while simultaneously printing 'M rows failed to score', so a reviewer sees fewer sampled rows than the scored+failed rows actually accounted for. sampled_rows should be captured from the input length BEFORE truncation (the number of rows actually submitted for scoring).
real.evidence: Repro output: `sampled_rows=1 scored_rows=1 failed_rows=1` then `invariant (sampled == scored + failed): False (1 == 1 + 1)`; AssertionError "BUG REPRODUCED: sampled_rows=1 (post-truncation length) but expected 2 (rows submitted for scoring)". Code trace: _impact.py:422 `failed = len(input_df) - scored` (ORIGINAL length) -> :427 `input_df = input_df.head(scored)` (truncates in place) -> :449 `sampled_rows=len(input_df)` reads the truncated length. The sibling first-deploy path in cli/_impact.py:141-143 sets sampled_rows=len(records), scored_rows=len(staging_preds), failed_rows=len(records)-len(staging_preds), establishing the intended invariant sampled==scored+failed which build_report violates. Both formatters (_impact.py:484-488 and 553-557) emit "(N of total sampled)" alongside "M rows failed to score", surfacing the contradiction to reviewers.
real.fix: Capture the submitted-row count before truncation and use it for sampled_rows. In build_report, before line 424's truncation, record `sampled = len(input_df)` (the number of rows submitted for scoring, equal to scored + failed), then pass `sampled_rows=sampled` at line 449 instead of `len(input_df)`. Leave `scored`/`failed` as-is. Add a regression assertion `report.sampled_rows == 2` (and the invariant `sampled_rows == scored_rows + failed_rows`) to the existing test_failed_rows_counted in tests/test_impact.py, which currently only checks scored_rows/failed_rows.

real.title: build_report only aligns input_df to predictions when staging != prod length, causing an unhandled ShapeError (and negative failed_rows) when equal-length predictions are shorter than input_df
real.description: The truncation guard at line 424 keys input_df alignment off `len(staging_preds) != len(prod_preds)` rather than off `scored < len(input_df)`. If staging and production predictions unwrap to the SAME length L but L < len(input_df) (e.g. both endpoints/envelopes return the same reduced row count, or an endpoint returns fewer predictions than inputs), input_df is left at its original length while stg_df/prd_df have L rows. _segment_breakdown (line 360) then builds pl.DataFrame({'seg': input_df[col], 'chg': change, ...}) with mismatched column heights and raises an unhandled polars ShapeError instead of a domain error or a consistent truncation. The same mismatch also makes `failed = len(input_df) - scored` correct only when truncation occurs; here failed stays positive but input_df is never trimmed, so segments crash. The fix is to always set input_df/preds to `scored` (and capture sampled_rows beforehand) regardless of staging-vs-prod equality.
