real.title: Linear chain validation checks full node_map, not the routing-pruned set, so a pruned/non-ancestor parent is silently dropped from wiring
real.description: build_linear_execution_chain_functions validates base_node_id and chain_node_ids membership against node_map returned by _prepare_graph, raising ValueError('... not in the prepared graph') for anything missing. But _prepare_graph returns prepared.node_map == graph.node_map (the FULL graph: see projection.prepare_graph lines 2116/2130), whereas the actual wiring downstream relies on id_to_name, which contains ONLY the nodes in `order` = topo-sort of `needed` (ancestors of target_node_id that survived live-switch/source pruning; projection.py:2126-2128). The 'missing' check therefore does not match its stated contract: a node that is present in node_map but absent from id_to_name (because it was pruned by prune_live_switch_edges under routing_source='batch', or is simply not an ancestor of target_node_id) passes the check. It is then passed to _build_funcs as a chain parent via chain_parents, and _build_funcs computes src_ids = [pid for pid in parents_of.get(nid, []) if pid in id_to_name] (_execute_lazy.py:1475). Because the parent is filtered out by `if pid in id_to_name`, the first chain node is built with an EMPTY source list and no error is raised — a silently mis-wired chain that produces a wrong frame instead of failing loudly. The sole current caller (_optimiser_service.py:3967) derives base/chain as single-parent ancestors of body.node_id, so it is usually safe, but a source/live-switch-pruned branch under routing_source='batch' can still remove a chain node from id_to_name while leaving it in node_map, making this reachable. The validation should be performed against the routing-scoped set (id_to_name / order), not the full node_map, so a chain node that did not survive routing fails loudly.
real.evidence: Repro output: `raised: None` and `recorded: {'chain0': {'source_names': [], 'source_ids': []}}`. The public API build_linear_execution_chain_functions accepted base_node_id="base" (present in graph.node_map but NOT an ancestor of target_node_id="target", hence absent from id_to_name), did NOT raise, and built the first chain node with an EMPTY source list. Code trace: execution.py:752 `missing = [n for n in (base_node_id,*chain_ids) if n not in node_map]` checks the FULL node_map (projection.py:2116 `node_map = graph.node_map`), whereas _execute_lazy.py:1475 `src_ids = [pid for pid in parents_of.get(nid, []) if pid in id_to_name]` silently drops any parent absent from the routing-scoped id_to_name (projection.py:2128, scoped to ancestors of target_node_id post-prune). The chain_parents wiring (execution.py:759-763) makes base the declared parent of chain0; that parent is filtered out -> empty source_names, no error.
real.fix: Validate base_node_id/chain_node_ids against the routing-scoped set, not the full node_map. In build_linear_execution_chain_functions (execution.py:752) change the membership test to `if node_id not in id_to_name` (the dict returned alongside node_map from _prepare_graph), so any base/chain node that did not survive routing/pruning fails loudly with the existing ValueError instead of being silently dropped to an empty source list in _build_funcs. Add a direct unit test for this public API (none exists today) covering: (a) a base/chain node absent from id_to_name now raises ValueError, and (b) the happy path still wires chain_parents correctly. The chain_id node_map[chain_id].data.nodeType lookups at lines 765-773 still use node_map and remain valid since survivors are a subset of node_map.

real.title: safe_joblib_load captures original_find_class OUTSIDE the lock, permanently leaking a restricted find_class onto NumpyUnpickler under concurrent loads
real.description: safe_joblib_load monkeypatches NumpyUnpickler.find_class with a restricted closure inside `with _joblib_lock`, then restores `original_find_class` in finally. But `original_find_class = NumpyUnpickler.find_class` is read at line 452, OUTSIDE the lock. If thread B enters safe_joblib_load while thread A holds the lock (A has already replaced find_class with its restricted closure), B captures A's restricted function as its 'original'. When B later acquires the lock, runs, and hits its finally, it restores find_class to A's restricted closure rather than the genuine NumpyUnpickler.find_class. The result is that after the interleaving, NumpyUnpickler.find_class is left permanently pointing at a dead `safe_joblib_load.<locals>._restricted_joblib_find_class`, so EVERY subsequent joblib.load process-wide (including plain joblib.load calls outside the sandbox) silently uses a restricted find_class belonging to a leaked closure. Repeated races can also stack nested restricted wrappers. The single-threaded tests (test_safe_load_does_not_break_subsequent_loads, test_safe_load_restored_after_error) do not cover this concurrent path. Reachable via _io.load_external_object(file_type='joblib'), which servers can invoke concurrently for model loading.
real.evidence: Deterministic repro output: "joblib.load call count: 2"; "final is genuine pickle._Unpickler.find_class (RESTORED): False"; "final is a LEAKED _restricted_joblib_find_class closure: True"; final repr = "<function safe_joblib_load.<locals>._restricted_joblib_find_class at 0x...>". After the forced interleaving (A patches + holds lock; B reads line 452 == A's restricted closure; B parks on lock; A restores genuine + releases; B then restores A's restricted closure in its finally), NumpyUnpickler.find_class is permanently left bound to thread A's dead closure instead of pickle._Unpickler.find_class. Code-trace confirms src/haute/_sandbox.py:452 `original_find_class = NumpyUnpickler.find_class` is the SOLE capture and lies OUTSIDE `with _joblib_lock` at line 465; it is the only patcher/restorer of NumpyUnpickler.find_class (grep confirmed), so nothing else restores the genuine method.
real.fix: Move the capture inside the lock so the genuine value is always read while no other thread can have patched it: delete line 452 and, immediately after `with _joblib_lock:` (line 465), do `original_find_class = NumpyUnpickler.find_class` before installing the restricted closure. Because the patch/restore are both serialized by `_joblib_lock`, reading the original under the lock guarantees it is `pickle._Unpickler.find_class`. (The nested `_restricted_joblib_find_class` must then close over a value assigned before its definition — define the closure inside the lock too, or restore explicitly to a module-level `_GENUINE_NUMPY_FIND_CLASS = pickle._Unpickler.find_class` captured once at import.) Add a concurrency regression test that interleaves two safe_joblib_load calls (e.g. via an instrumented lock as in the repro) and asserts NumpyUnpickler.find_class is pickle._Unpickler.find_class afterwards.

real.title: Parse-time contract fallback swallows ImportError/RuntimeError that the runtime boundary check was deliberately narrowed to re-raise (silent-failure drift)
real.description: Both _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (line 268: `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]`) and the live predicate _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 284: `isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError))`) treat ImportError and RuntimeError as recoverable 'fall back to opaque contract' conditions. Their docstrings explicitly claim they mirror the runtime boundary check: line 262-263 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy._BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS`` — the parse-time fallback must not swallow more than the runtime boundary check would', and line 281-282 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy``'. That invariant is now VIOLATED. The runtime sibling (_execute_lazy._compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception) was deliberately narrowed in commit 34aff403 ('Phase 3 audit — narrow 4 exception catches') from `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` down to `(ConfigError, OSError, MlflowException)`, with a detailed rationale in its docstring (_execute_lazy.py:140-150): RuntimeError ('Persistently corrupt model artifact' from _load_with_bounded_retry) and ImportError (missing catboost/rustystats backend) are real deploy/infra bugs that must surface loudly, NOT be silently downgraded to an opaque contract. The parse-time copy in _config_builder.py was not updated in that commit (34aff403 touched only _execute_lazy.py), so it still carries the old wide set. Consequence: if a node declares `contract=...` and _derive_parse_time_contract raises ImportError or RuntimeError (e.g. a contract function that imports an optional backend, or a corrupt-artifact RuntimeError), _validate_user_contract (line 334-346) catches it and silently treats the builder as fully opaque (Contract.opaque()), so a genuinely drifted/wrong user contract annotation passes parse-time validation unflagged — exactly the silencing the runtime narrowing was meant to prevent. The referenced symbol `_BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS` in the docstring does not even exist (the real names are _compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception), confirming the docstring drifted from reality.
real.evidence: Repro output (exit 0): "ImportError   parse-time swallow=True  runtime swallow=False" and "RuntimeError  parse-time swallow=True  runtime swallow=False"; "parse-time tuple : ('ConfigError','OSError','ImportError','RuntimeError','MlflowException')" vs "runtime tuple : ('ConfigError','OSError','MlflowException')"; "_execute_lazy._BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS exists = False"; Part 3 "derivation raises ImportError -> _validate_user_contract SWALLOWED (no error)" and likewise RuntimeError. Source confirms: _config_builder.py:268/:284 use (ConfigError,OSError,ImportError,RuntimeError)+MlflowException while _execute_lazy.py:157/:171 use (ConfigError,OSError)+MlflowException. git show 34aff403 --stat lists only src/haute/_execute_lazy.py (config_builder untouched); the diff replaces `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` with `[ConfigError, OSError]`. The parse-time set is a strict superset, violating its own docstring invariant (_config_builder.py:262-263 "must not swallow more than the runtime boundary check would") and referencing a non-existent symbol _BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS.
real.fix: Mirror commit 34aff403 in _config_builder.py: in _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (line 268) change the base list to `[ConfigError, OSError]` (MlflowException still appended when importable), and in _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 284) change the isinstance check to `isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError))`. Update both docstrings (lines 262-263, 281-282) to reference the real runtime symbols `_compute_boundary_check_exceptions` / `_is_boundary_check_exception` instead of the non-existent `_BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS`. Add a parity unit test that asserts `_compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions() == _compute_boundary_check_exceptions()` and that both predicates agree on ImportError/RuntimeError, so the two sets can never silently drift again.

real.title: stop_reason() returning 'completed' raises an uncaught ValueError and silently skips cleanup callbacks
real.description: stop_reason is typed Callable[[], WorkerTerminalReason | None], and 'completed' is a member of WorkerTerminalReason. If a caller's stop_reason returns 'completed', _wait_for_worker first calls _terminate_process(process) (killing the worker) and then constructs IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason='completed'), whose __init__ raises ValueError('completed is not a valid stopped-worker reason'). That ValueError is NOT an IsolatedWorkerError, so the 'except IsolatedWorkerError' arm in run_isolated_worker (line 236) does not catch it. It propagates out through the finally (queue closed) and skips the entire cleanup section (lines 245-251) -> parent-owned cleanup_callbacks never run, contradicting the module contract that 'the parent ... always runs them after the child reaches a terminal state' (lines 178-180). The validation that rejects 'completed' is placed in the exception constructor (after termination) instead of where stop_reason is read, turning a guard into a cleanup-bypassing crash.
real.evidence: Repro output (exit 0): bug case `stop_reason()->'completed'` -> `raised -> ValueError: completed is not a valid stopped-worker reason`; `isinstance IsolatedWorkerError -> False`; `cleanup_ran -> False`. Control case `stop_reason()->'cancelled'` -> `IsolatedWorkerStoppedError` with `cleanup_ran -> True`. Code: _worker_isolation.py L17-25 WorkerTerminalReason includes "completed"; L36 stop_reason typed `Callable[[], WorkerTerminalReason | None]`; L332-334 `if reason is not None: _terminate_process(process); raise IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason=reason)`; L116-117 constructor does `if terminal_reason == "completed": raise ValueError(...)` BEFORE super().__init__, so the object is a bare ValueError (not IsolatedWorkerError). run_isolated_worker L236 `except IsolatedWorkerError` does not match -> ValueError passes through the L238-243 finally and skips the cleanup section L245-251, so _run_cleanup_callbacks never runs.
real.fix: The validation is misplaced: it lives in IsolatedWorkerStoppedError.__init__ (after _terminate_process already killed the worker) and produces a ValueError that is neither an IsolatedWorkerError nor cleanup-safe. Make the invalid value unrepresentable: introduce a dedicated `WorkerStopReason` Literal that EXCLUDES "completed" (e.g. superseded/timed_out/cancelled/memory_limited/contract_error/error) and type `stop_reason: Callable[[], WorkerStopReason | None]`, then drop the runtime `if terminal_reason == "completed"` branch from the constructor. Alternatively (minimal), validate at the read site in _wait_for_worker before terminating: if stop_reason() returns "completed", raise a typed IsolatedWorkerError subclass (a contract_error) so the existing `except IsolatedWorkerError` arm still catches it and the parent-owned cleanup callbacks at lines 245-251 always run. Add a unit test asserting both that a typed IsolatedWorkerError (not a bare ValueError) propagates and that cleanup_callbacks execute for the "completed" stop_reason input.

real.title: build_and_push_image reuses a non-cleared .haute_build dir, baking stale artifacts from a prior run into the new image
real.description: The build dir is created with `build_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` and `artifacts_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, and is only removed in the `except BaseException` cleanup (lines 165-167). A SUCCESSFUL build therefore leaves `.haute_build/` (and `.haute_build/artifacts/`) on disk. A subsequent `build_and_push_image` call in the same working directory reuses that directory without clearing it: the manifest, Dockerfile and app.py are overwritten, but artifact files are only ever *added* (`shutil.copy2(artifact_path, artifacts_dir / artifact_name)`), never pruned. If the artifact set changes between runs (e.g. a model file is renamed, or a `.pkl` is replaced by a `.cbm`), the orphaned file from the previous run survives and is copied wholesale into the image by the Dockerfile's directory-level `COPY artifacts/ artifacts/` (line 471). The result is a container that silently ships a stale model artifact that is not referenced by the current manifest. Note the sibling MLflow path (`_mlflow.py`) is immune because it logs the live `artifact_path`s rather than copying into a reused directory, so this staleness is specific to the container target's copy+COPY model.
real.evidence: Repro output: "artifacts/ on disk after run 2 : ['new_model.cbm', 'old_model.cbm']" while "manifest['artifacts'] after run2: ['new_model.cbm']". The run-1 orphan old_model.cbm (bytes='OLD MODEL BYTES') survives in .haute_build/artifacts/ after a second build that switched the artifact set, yet the freshly written manifest references only new_model.cbm. Code trace: line 98 build_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True) and line 102 artifacts_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True) reuse without clearing; lines 121-124 only copy current artifacts in (never prune); cleanup shutil.rmtree at line 166 sits solely in the `except BaseException` branch, so a successful build leaves the dir on disk for the next invocation; line 471 `COPY artifacts/ artifacts/` then bundles the whole directory, including the orphan, into the image. grep confirms no other rmtree/guard for .haute_build in _container.py; sibling _mlflow.py copies nothing into the reused dir (logs live artifact_paths) so it is unaffected, exactly as the finding states.
real.fix: Clear the build directory before (re)creating it so each run starts from a clean tree: at the top of build_and_push_image replace `build_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` with `shutil.rmtree(build_dir, ignore_errors=True)` followed by `build_dir.mkdir()` (then artifacts_dir.mkdir() inside the try). This is the minimal, consistent fix and preserves the existing `except BaseException` rmtree for partial-failure cleanup. Add a regression test that runs build_and_push_image twice in the same cwd with differing artifact sets (model_a.cbm then model_b.cbm) and asserts `.haute_build/artifacts/` contains exactly the current run's files.

real.title: Sync-banner close button renders mojibake "â€¢" instead of an ✕ icon (double-encoded character on disk)
real.description: The dismiss button for the WebSocket sync-error banner has its label corrupted on disk. The on-disk bytes are `C3 A2 C5 93 E2 80 A2`, which is the UTF-8 encoding of three code points U+00E2 (â) U+0153 (œ) U+2022 (•) — i.e. the literal string "â€¢". This is a classic double-encoding of the intended close glyph U+2715 (✕, MULTIPLICATION X, correct UTF-8 `E2 9C 95`): the original `E2 9C 95` was decoded as Windows-1252 (E2→â, 9C→œ, 95→•) and re-saved as UTF-8. The button therefore displays the garbage string "â€¢" to the user rather than a close icon, in a banner that appears precisely when sync has failed (a stressful, visible moment). The directly-above sessionExpired banner uses a text "Reload" button and is unaffected, so only this control is broken — meaning the regression is easy to miss in review since the surrounding chrome looks fine.
real.evidence: App.tsx:537 text node between `opacity-100">` and `</button>` has on-disk bytes `c3 a2 c5 93 e2 80 a2` (verified via uv run python). UTF-8 decode = codepoints [0xe2 'â', 0x153 'œ', 0x2022 '•'] = literal "â€¢"; the intended ✕ U+2715 is absent (contains-U+2715 == False). Double-encoding proven exact: '✕'.encode('utf-8') = e2 9c 95 → decode cp1252 → re-encode utf-8 = c3 a2 c5 93 e2 80 a2 (byte-for-byte match). File is valid UTF-8 with no BOM, so Vite/esbuild preserves the literal verbatim into a 3-char DOM text node. Uniqueness verified: lines 69/94/120/191/196/210 are also mojibake but all inside `//` comments; 332/337/357 are legitimate single U+2014 em-dashes; line 537 is the ONLY mojibake in rendered JSX. User-facing path confirmed: syncBanner is set on real WS sync failures (useWebSocketSync.ts:139 unsaved-changes-on-disk, :359 `msg.error||"Parse error in pipeline file"`); when truthy, App.tsx:533-538 renders the banner with this corrupted close button.
real.fix: Replace the corrupted literal "â€¢" on App.tsx:537 with the intended close glyph. Prefer consistency with the rest of the file, which uses lucide-react icons (e.g. PanelLeftOpen at line 512): import { X } from "lucide-react" and render `<X size={14} />` inside the button (add an aria-label="Dismiss"). If keeping a text glyph, use a proper ✕ (U+2715) or × (U+00D7) saved as correct UTF-8. Add a CI guard (lint/test) that fails on the byte sequences `c3 a2`/`c5 93` (mojibake leads) in rendered JSX, or a repo-wide mojibake scanner, to prevent regressions.

real.title: "Unmatched rows" counter can go negative because match counts are summed across independently-counted (possibly overlapping) rules
real.description: The per-rule match counts are computed by counting, for EACH rule, every preview row that satisfies that rule independently (lines 142-168). `matchedRows` is then `matchCounts.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0)` and `unmatchedCount = totalRows - matchedRows` (lines 172-173), with no clamping. When two or more continuous rules overlap, a single row is counted once per matching rule, so `matchedRows` can exceed `totalRows`, making `unmatchedCount` negative. The Default counter at line 554 then renders e.g. "-2 of 100 rows". Overlapping continuous rules are an explicitly supported and merely warned-about state (see warnings block lines 193-198 and detectOverlaps). The backend never double-counts: src/haute/_rating.py _apply_banding builds a when/then chain (first-match-wins, lines 119-133), so a row is assigned by exactly one rule. The preview model (count-each-rule) therefore diverges from real assignment semantics and produces an impossible negative unmatched figure.
real.evidence: BandingEditor.tsx:172 `matchedRows = matchCounts.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0)`; :173 `unmatchedCount = totalRows - matchedRows` (no clamp); :549 render guard `matchCounts && totalRows > 0`; :554 renders `{unmatchedCount} of {totalRows} rows`; :552 color uses `unmatchedCount === 0 ? success : warning-strong`. Continuous match counting is per-rule independent (:161-168) via matchesContinuousRule. In bandingUtils.ts parseRuleInterval+matchesContinuousRule(:216-227): for value 12, rule A `<=15` → upper=15 incl, 12>15 false → matches; rule B `>=10 <=20` → lower=10/upper=20 incl, 12 in range → matches. So a single overlapping row is counted twice → matchCounts=[1,1], matchedRows=2, totalRows=1, unmatchedCount=1-2=-1 → renders "-1 of 1 rows". detectOverlaps (bandingUtils.ts:95-119, intervalsOverlap:81-93) returns the overlap only as a non-blocking warning — overlap is a supported state. Existing test BandingEditor.test.tsx:640-657 uses this exact overlapping pair [<=15 'A'],[>=10<=20 'B'] and asserts only the "overlap" warning (rendered WITHOUT previewRows), confirming overlap is intentionally allowed and the negative-counter path is untested/unguarded. Backend _rating.py:118-133 builds a pl.when/then first-match-wins chain → each row assigned by exactly one rule → true unmatched is always >=0, so the preview's count-each-rule figure diverges and can show an impossible negative.
real.fix: Clamp the displayed figure: `const unmatchedCount = Math.max(0, totalRows - matchedRows)` at BandingEditor.tsx:173, which removes the impossible negative. For a figure that is actually correct under overlap, compute matched rows with first-match-wins semantics mirroring the backend (count each previewRow once against the first rule that matches, e.g. `previewRows.filter(row => rules.some(r => matchesContinuousRule(Number(row[column]), r))).length`) instead of summing independent per-rule counts; then unmatched = totalRows - that count, always >=0. Add a regression test combining the overlapping-rules config (test lines 640-651) with previewRows containing a value in the overlap (e.g. {age:12}) and assert the counter is non-negative (e.g. "0 of 1").

real.title: Pattern grouping keeps only the first column's dtype; siblings with a different dtype are misrepresented by the row's dtype badge
real.description: buildGroups collapses columns that share a numeric-segment pattern (e.g. arr.0, arr.1 -> arr.*) into one PatternRow and records a single dtype. The dtype is captured once on first insertion into patternMap and never reconciled against later columns sharing the same pattern. When sibling columns under the same pattern have heterogeneous dtypes (entirely possible for struct/array-derived flattened columns, e.g. arr.0=Int64, arr.1=Float64), the collapsed row shows only the FIRST concrete column's dtype, silently hiding that the group mixes types.
real.evidence: GroupedColumnsTab.tsx:61 writes dtype ONLY in the `if (!patternMap.has(pat))` branch; :62 only pushes the name for subsequent same-pattern columns; :70 builds PatternRow.dtype = concreteColumns[0].dtype; :504-505 renders that single dtype via getDtypeColor(row.dtype). Isolated Node re-run of the pure logic (lines 20-78) on [{arr.0:Int64},{arr.1:Float64}] -> "collapsed row.dtype : Int64" while "actual sibling dtypes: [Int64,Float64]" -> BUG CONFIRMED (exit 0). No upstream guard: types/node.ts:6-9 ColumnInfo is arbitrary {name,dtype}; usePipelineAPI.ts:123-124 + 144-145 set _columns/_availableColumns verbatim from API with no dtype reconciliation; NodePanel.tsx:1022-1026 passes them straight in.
real.fix: In buildGroups, detect heterogeneous dtypes per pattern: when pushing a same-pattern column whose dtype differs from the stored one, mark the entry mixed (e.g. track a Set<string> of dtypes or a boolean). Propagate to PatternRow and, at the render site (503-507), show a neutral "mixed" badge (or list distinct dtypes) instead of concreteColumns[0]'s dtype so the type badge cannot misrepresent a multi-dtype group. Pure display change; no data/config impact.

real.title: FileBrowser cache-hit path does not clear a stale error, leaving a successfully-loaded directory hidden behind a stale error banner
real.description: In the FileBrowser effect, the cache-hit fast path (`if (cached) { setItems(...); setLoading(false); return }`) returns without calling `setError(null)`. Only the cache-miss branch resets the error (line 189). Because the render checks `error` BEFORE `items` (lines 250-251), a stale error from a previously-failed directory persists and masks the cached content of a different, successfully-loaded directory.
real.evidence:
_shared.tsx lines 183-189: `const cached = getFileListCache(cacheKey); if (cached) { setItems(cached as FileItem[]); setLoading(false); return }` then (only after the early return) `setError(null)` at line 189. The cache-HIT branch returns WITHOUT clearing `error`; only the cache-MISS branch calls setError(null). `error` is set to a message ONLY in the catch at line 200 and is never reset anywhere except line 189. Render at lines 248-252 evaluates `loading ? ... : error ?
{error}
: items.length===0 ? ... : items.map(...)` — error is checked BEFORE items, so a non-null error masks valid `items`. useSettingsStore.ts: setFileListCache is called ONLY on success (line 195); the catch (lines 198-203) never caches, so a failed dir is never cached; getFileListCache returns entry.items within a 30s TTL (line 194). goUp (lines 211-212) does setLoading(true) then setDir(parent), with no setError(null). Exact reachable trace: (1) dir B loads OK -> error=null,items=B, B cached. (2) click subdir A -> setDir(A); A cache-miss -> setError(null), listFiles(A) rejects -> catch sets error='', items=[]; A not cached. (3) click goUp -> setLoading(true), setDir(B). (4) effect for B -> getFileListCache('B|ext') HIT -> setItems(B), setLoading(false), return; setError(null) at line 189 is bypassed; error stays ''. (5) render: loading=false, error truthy -> shows A's stale error banner; B's valid cached rows in items are hidden until 30s TTL expiry or a cacheKey change to a miss. No guard elsewhere resets error on the cache-hit path.
real.fix: Clear the stale error on the cache-hit path. Simplest: hoist `setError(null)` above the cache check so it runs on every effect invocation (place it immediately after computing cacheKey, before `const cached = getFileListCache(...)`), or equivalently add `setError(null)` inside the `if (cached) { ... }` block before the `return`. Add a regression test in _shared.test.tsx (existing infra supports it): render FileBrowser; navigate into a subdir whose listFiles rejects (assert error text shown); then set mockGetFileListCache to return the parent's cached items and click the goUp/ChevronLeft button; assert the cached file name IS visible and the prior error text is NOT in the document.

real.title: InputSourcesBar uses non-unique varName as React key, causing key collisions and mis-targeted delete buttons when two upstream sources share a sanitized name
real.description: InputSourcesBar renders `inputSources.map((src) => <span key={src.varName} ...>)`. `varName` is NOT unique: in NodePanel.tsx (line 636) it is computed as `sanitizeName(nodeMap[e.source]?.data.label || e.source)`, derived from the upstream node label. sanitizeName is many-to-one, so distinct upstream nodes whose labels collapse to the same identifier produce identical `varName` values and therefore duplicate React keys. real.title: detectGaps reports spurious/incorrect gaps when continuous rules overlap or nest (uses predecessor upper, not running-max upper)
real.description: detectGaps sorts intervals by lower bound only, then in the loop compares each interval against its immediate successor using `curr.upper` (the predecessor's own upper) rather than the maximum upper bound seen so far. When an earlier-sorted interval has a wider/larger upper than a later one (i.e. the intervals overlap or one is contained in another), the comparison uses the narrower interval's upper and fabricates a gap that does not exist, or reports the wrong gap bounds. Because detectGaps is invoked only for `factor.banding === "continuous"` (hand-authored rules in BandingEditor.tsx:199), where a user can freely author overlapping/nested ranges, this surfaces a false validation warning directly to the user.
real.evidence: detectGaps (bandingUtils.ts:146-158) loops `for (i=0; i<len-1; i++)` comparing `curr=intervals[i].interval` vs `next=intervals[i+1].interval` using `curr.upper`, never a running-max upper. Trace for evidence rules A[0,100], B[10,20], C[200,∞): sort comparator `aLo-bLo` (0,10,200) yields order A,B,C. i=1: curr=B(upper=20), next=C(lower=200); line 153 `curr.upper(20) < next.lower(200)` is TRUE → pushes "Gap between 20 and 200". True coverage [0,100]∪[10,20]∪[200,∞) = [0,100]∪[200,∞); the only real gap is (100,200). The message states a demonstrably WRONG bound (20 instead of 100) and frames a gap starting inside covered territory. Because B is nested in A, B's narrow upper (20) is wrongly carried forward instead of A's upper (100). BandingEditor.tsx:199-202 pushes this string straight into the user-facing `w` warnings under `factor.banding === "continuous"` (line 186), where users freely author overlapping/nested ranges. No guard suppresses it: detectGaps runs unconditionally; detectOverlaps fires independently and does not gate the gap push. Existing tests (bandingUtils.test.ts:151-209) only cover DISJOINT intervals where predecessor-upper == running-max-upper, so the bug is uncovered.
real.fix: Carry a running maximum upper bound (with inclusivity) across the sorted intervals instead of comparing only adjacent `intervals[i].interval.upper`. E.g. track `coveredUpper`/`coveredUpperInclusive` initialised from the first interval, and for each subsequent interval compare `next.lower` against `coveredUpper`; if `next.upper` (or null=+∞) extends coverage, advance `coveredUpper`. Treat any `upper===null` as +∞ (full coverage from that point). Add tests for: nested interval followed by a disjoint one (A[0,100],B[10,20],C[200,∞) → exactly one gap "(100,200)", NOT "20..200"); fully nested with no later interval (A[0,100],B[10,20] → no gap); overlapping-then-gap chains. Keep behaviour_preservation: disjoint cases must still report the same gaps.

real.title: Stale pageIndex not reconciled when report prop shrinks; Previous button needs multiple clicks
real.description: pageIndex is held in state but only clamped at render time via currentPageIndex = Math.min(pageIndex, pageCount - 1). The clamp never writes back to state. When the report prop changes to one with fewer pages (e.g. user explores a 200-column dataset, pages to page 3, then explores a 60-column dataset), the SchemaTableCard instance is NOT remounted (ExploreOverviewPane keys it by the static card.key 'schema', not by node/report id - see ExploreOverviewPane.tsx:101-103), so pageIndex stays 3 while pageCount drops to e.g. 2. But the Previous onClick does setPageIndex(current => Math.max(current - 1, 0)) operating on the raw stale value (3 -> 2), so currentPageIndex stays Math.min(2, 1) = 1 and the visible page does not change. The user must click Previous repeatedly (3 -> 2 -> 1) before raw pageIndex falls within range and the page actually moves. The Previous button is effectively dead for the first N-(pageCount-1) clicks.

real.title: Best-iteration reference line treats best_iteration as an array index, misplacing it when loss_history is truncated
real.description: `bestX` is computed as `xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1))`, but `xScale(i) = marginLeft + (i / (length-1)) * chartW` interprets its argument as a 0-based ARRAY INDEX into `lossHistory`, whereas `result.best_iteration` is the model's actual ITERATION NUMBER. The backend (`_train_service.py` `_bounded_loss_history`, default `HAUTE_TRAIN_LOSS_HISTORY_LIMIT=200`) keeps only the last 200 rows (`history[-200:]`) for runs longer than 200 iterations, so the window slides and `lossHistory[0].iteration` is non-zero (e.g. iterations 700..899 for a 900-iteration run). Locate the visible-window array index via `const bestIdx = lossHistory.findIndex(e => e.iteration === bestIteration)` and set `bestX = (isFiniteNumber(bestIteration) && bestIdx >= 0) ? xScale(bestIdx) : null`, so the dashed line and its legend entry are hidden when best_iteration is not in the truncated window. Separately, reconcile the latent off-by-one: the loss_history `iteration` field is 1-based (it=info.iteration+1) while best_iteration is CatBoost's 0-based best_iteration_; align them (e.g. record best_iteration as +1, or match on the consistent basis) so even untruncated runs place the line on the exact best column.

real.title: CI whiskers can overflow the bar container because maxDev ignores confidence-interval bounds
real.description: The horizontal scale `maxDev` is derived ONLY from each term's point deviation `|relativity - 1|` (with a 0.1 floor). The confidence-interval whiskers are then positioned/sized against this same `maxDev`. Because a relativity's CI is frequently WIDER than the largest point-deviation across the displayed terms, `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` routinely fall outside the `[1 - maxDev, 1 + maxDev]` range, producing a whisker with negative `left` (overflowing left, past the feature-name column) and/or `width` > 100% (extending past the right edge). The bar container (line 91, `className="flex-1 h-4 relative"`) has no `overflow: hidden`, so the overflow is visible and the whisker is clipped/misplaced, misrepresenting the displayed uncertainty.
real.evidence: GLMRelativitiesTab.tsx:45 `maxDev = Math.max(rows.map(r => Math.abs(r.relativity - 1)).reduce(...), 0.1)` uses ONLY point deviations. Lines 116-117 scale the whisker against the same maxDev: `left: ${50 + ((row.ci_lower - 1) / maxDev) * 50}%`, `width: ${((row.ci_upper - row.ci_lower) / maxDev) * 50}%`. Computed against the repo's own committed fixture (GLMComponents.test.tsx:65-68, maxDev=0.709): (Intercept) CI[0.265,0.32] -> left=-1.83% (negative -> overflows left under the 140px feature-name column). Finder's worked example (rel=1.05, CI[0.7,1.5], maxDev floored to 0.1) -> left=-100%, width=400%, right=300%. The point bar never overflows: pct=(|dev|/maxDev)*50 and maxDev>=|dev| so pct<=50, keeping bars in [0,100]%. The per-row bar container (line 91 `flex-1 h-4 relative`) has NO overflow property; the only overflow rule is `overflow-y-auto` on the distinct outer scroller (line 72), which cannot recover a whisker rendered at a negative left offset overlapping the sibling label. ci_lower/ci_upper are independent exponentiated CI bounds (parsed as plain finite numbers in guards.ts:1047-1048; computed as exp(conf_int) in _rustystats.py:430-431) with no relation to maxDev, so no guard prevents the overflow.
real.fix: Either (a) clamp the whisker endpoints to the bar box before rendering — compute `lo = Math.max(0, 50 + ((ci_lower-1)/maxDev)*50)`, `hi = Math.min(100, 50 + ((ci_upper-1)/maxDev)*50)`, set `left:lo%`, `width:(hi-lo)%` — and/or (b) include the CI bounds when deriving the scale, e.g. `maxDev = Math.max(0.1, ...rows.flatMap(r => [Math.abs(r.relativity-1), r.ci_lower!=null?Math.abs(r.ci_lower-1):0, r.ci_upper!=null?Math.abs(r.ci_upper-1):0]))`, so the whole CI fits in [1-maxDev,1+maxDev]. Option (b) preserves the full whisker proportionally and is preferable for correctness; combining with `overflow-hidden` on the line-91 container is a cheap defensive backstop. Add a unit test asserting the rendered whisker `left>=0` and `left+width<=100` for a row whose CI is wider than the largest point deviation.

real.title: FeatureImportance maxVal uses items[0].importance, wrong for negative/zero importances
real.description: maxVal is taken as `items[0]?.importance || 1` on the assumption that the first (descending-sorted) feature is the largest by magnitude. Bar width is then `(Math.abs(fi.importance) / Math.abs(maxVal)) * 100%` (line 60), which uses absolute values. The backend sorts feature_importance / feature_importance_loss by RAW value descending, not by absolute value (src/haute/modelling/_algorithms.py:620-624 and 639-643 `sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)`), and CatBoost LossFunctionChange importances can be negative (no abs/clip applied; _result_types.py:19). Consequences on the 'Loss' tab: (a) a feature with a large NEGATIVE importance sorts LAST, so its |importance| can exceed |items[0].importance|, yielding a bar width > 100% (overflow); (b) if items[0].importance is itself negative, Math.abs(maxVal) is a small positive denominator and ALL bars are massively over-scaled; (c) if items[0].importance === 0, `0 || 1` forces maxVal=1, mis-scaling every bar. The hardened sibling FeaturesTab.tsx computes `maxVal = items.map(i => Math.abs(i.importance)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b), -Infinity)` (FeaturesTab.tsx:46) and guards the denominator with `maxVal > 0 ? ... : '0%'` (FeaturesTab.tsx:91). Existing FeatureImportance tests only use positive descending importances, so this is uncovered.
real.evidence: FeatureImportance.tsx:28 `const maxVal = items[0]?.importance || 1` + :60 `width: ${(Math.abs(fi.importance)/Math.abs(maxVal))*100}%`. Backend _algorithms.py:639-644 sorts `feature_importance_typed` pairs `key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True` (RAW value desc) and stores `float(imp)` with no abs/clip; _training_job.py:1206-1210 populates feature_importance_loss via `LossFunctionChange` (a signed quantity — negative for features whose removal lowers loss). So items[0] is the max RAW value, not max magnitude. Counterexample items=[{imp:2},{imp:-50}] -> maxVal=2 -> the -50 bar = Math.abs(-50)/Math.abs(2)*100 = 2500% (mode a). items=[{imp:-1},{imp:-3}] -> maxVal=-1 -> -3 bar = 300% (mode b). items[0].importance===0 -> `0||1` forces maxVal=1 -> every bar scaled against arbitrary unit-1 (mode c). Sibling FeaturesTab.tsx:46 uses `items.map(i=>Math.abs(i.importance)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b),-Infinity)` and :91 guards `maxVal>0 ? ... : '0%'` — the correct pattern, absent here. FeatureImportance.test.tsx uses only positive descending importances (10/8, 5/3, 15..1), so all three modes are uncovered.
real.fix: In FeatureImportance.tsx, replace line 28 with the magnitude-max pattern already used in FeaturesTab.tsx and guard the denominator. E.g. `const maxVal = items.reduce((m, i) => Math.max(m, Math.abs(i.importance)), 0)` and at line 60 use `width: maxVal > 0 ? `${(Math.abs(fi.importance) / maxVal) * 100}%` : "0%"`. This makes bar widths correct regardless of sort order, sign, or a zero-valued first element. Add FeatureImportance.test.tsx cases on the Loss tab covering: a large negative importance sorted last (assert width <= 100%), all-negative importances, and a zero importance, mirroring how FeaturesTab handles them; consider extracting the shared scaling helper to avoid the divergence recurring.

real.title: CancellableJobRegistry entry leaks when training-job construction fails in _launch_background
real.description: _launch_background calls self._training_jobs.register_latest(...) at line 1043 (registering a JobCancellation token under key (_TRAINING_JOB_TYPE, job_id)), then performs an atomic_update (1048), build_training_job_kwargs (1092) and TrainingJob(**job_kwargs) (1097) BEFORE the thread-start try-block at line 1232. If any of those raise, the registry token is never released: the worker thread's finally (which calls _training_jobs.release at 1227) never runs because the thread was never started, and the thread-start except (which calls release at 1245) is not reached because the exception is raised before entering the try at 1232. The exception propagates to start(), whose except/finally only call execution_context.release_admission() (lines 588-589) and JobLifecycle.transition() to 'error' — start() never touches self._training_jobs. Because register_latest keys on the unique job_id, the stale entry is never superseded by a later job (different key) and is never TTL-evicted (CancellableJobRegistry has no TTL; only JobStore does), so _tokens_by_job_id and _latest_by_key grow unboundedly. cancel()/timeout() cannot clean it up later either: the job is already terminal ('error'), so cancel() returns early at lines 598-599 without releasing, and timeout() is only driven for running jobs.
real.evidence: Repro output: raised TypeError: SplitConfig.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'definitely_not_a_split_field' (construction at _train_service.py:1097, before thread-start try at 1232); then `_tokens_by_job_id has job_id: True (expected False)`, `_latest_by_key has key: True (expected False)`, `_tokens_by_job_id size after 2nd failed launch: 2 (expected 0)`, and `still leaked after cancel(): True (expected False)`. The token registered by register_latest (line 1043) is never released; a second distinct job does not supersede it (unique key (_TRAINING_JOB_TYPE, job_id)), and cancel() returns early once the job is terminal ('error'). Confirmed by code-trace: start()'s except branches (533-586) only call _lifecycle.transition and its finally (587-589) only calls execution_context.release_admission() when not launch_started — never self._training_jobs.release; CancellableJobRegistry (_background_jobs.py:52-115) has no TTL eviction, only release() removes entries.
real.fix: Make _launch_background release the registry token on any failure before the worker thread is running. Wrap the body from register_latest (1043) through TrainingJob(**job_kwargs) (1097) and the thread start (1232-1234) so that if anything raises before the worker thread takes ownership, self._training_jobs.release(job_id) is called. Concretely: move register_latest into (or guard it with) a try whose except calls self._training_jobs.release(job_id) and execution_context.release_admission(), then re-raises — mirroring the existing thread-start except at 1235-1250 but covering the construction window too. Alternatively, register_latest only immediately before thread.start() (after job_kwargs/TrainingJob succeed), so a construction failure never registers a token. Add a regression test asserting service._training_jobs._tokens_by_job_id is empty after _launch_background raises on a malformed split / conflicting GLM var_power config.

Code containing only df.filter(segment='A') has no rename/select/derived-reference, so _single_parent_polars_expression_demands routes it straight to the unordered walk (not the ordered one), returning a parent demand that omits `segment`. compute_prepared_plan writes routed_demands.by_parent verbatim into edge_demands (projection.py:2253-2256), so the parent scan is narrowed to exclude `segment`; the filter then fails at execution with ColumnNotFoundError on otherwise-valid user code (or, if the column is genuinely present upstream and pruned, the filter loses a required input). In `_unordered_expression_demands` filter branch (projection.py:1212-1218), after `refs = _referenced_polars_columns(ast_node)` and the None-guard, also collect keyword-named columns: bail if any `kw.arg is None` (mirroring line 1119 — `**kwargs` is unknowable), then add `kw_cols = {kw.arg for kw in ast_node.keywords if kw.arg is not None}` to both `referenced_columns` and `demands` (e.g. `referenced_columns |= refs | kw_cols; demands |= refs | kw_cols`). Add a TDD failing test at the rule level: `SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule().parent_demands(node=<polars node code="df = df.filter(segment='A')">, parent_ids=['p1'], my_needed={'premium'})` must return by_parent={'p1': {'premium','segment'}}, plus the mixed with_columns+filter(seg='B') case expecting {'x','seg'}. refuted.title: Strip-prefix can author a column_renames entry whose target collides with an existing column, producing a runtime Polars duplicate-name error with no UI guard
refuted.description: Stripping a group prefix (or a mid segment) writes column_renames[old] = stripped without checking that `stripped` does not collide with another existing (non-renamed) column. The backend (_execute_lazy._apply_column_renames) builds `valid = {old:new for ... if old in all_cols and old != new}` then calls `frame.rename(valid)`; if two columns end up mapped to the same target, or a rename target equals an untouched existing column name, Polars raises a DuplicateError when the node runs. Because stripGroupPrefix only iterates the rows of one ColumnGroup, it cannot see a same-named column living in a different top-level group, so cross-group collisions are entirely unguarded. The UI lets the user author this invalid config and surfaces the failure only at execution time.
refuted.evidence: REFUTING GUARD: GroupedColumnsTab (which hosts stripGroupPrefix/toggleSegmentStrip) is rendered at exactly ONE production site, NodePanel.tsx:1021-1027, and ONLY for `nodeType === NODE_TYPES.API_INPUT`. That render is gated by the outer condition at NodePanel.tsx:1020 `{activeTab === "columns" && showColumnsTab ? ...}`. showColumnsTab is defined at NodePanel.tsx:666 as `isKnownNodeType && !isInstance && !NO_COLUMNS_TAB.has(nodeType)`, and NO_COLUMNS_TAB (NodePanel.tsx:72-79) CONTAINS NODE_TYPES.API_INPUT (line 73). nodeType is one `const` (line 664) used at both line 666 and line 1021. Therefore rendering GroupedColumnsTab requires nodeType===API_INPUT (line 1021) AND nodeType!==API_INPUT (via showColumnsTab) simultaneously — mutually exclusive. The component is unreachable dead code: for apiInput, showColumnsTab is false, so even the "columns" tab button (line 920 `{showColumnsTab && ...}`) never renders and activeTab can never become "columns". Pinned by frontend/src/__tests__/editors/apiInputBundle3aContract.test.tsx:117-134 ("does NOT render the Columns tab button for an apiInput node"). Grep confirms NodePanel.tsx:1022 is the only non-test, non-lazy-import reference to GroupedColumnsTab. CONSEQUENCE: a user cannot invoke stripGroupPrefix via the live UI, so the colliding column_renames entry (`licence.type -> type`) cannot be authored through this component — the finding's core premise ("The UI lets the user author this invalid config") is false. SEPARATE NUANCE (honesty): the backend behavioral sub-claim IS technically true and INTENTIONAL — `uv run python -c` over `pl.LazyFrame({'licence.type':[1],'type':[2]}).rename({'licence.type':'type'}).collect()` raises `DuplicateError: column 'type' is duplicate`, and _execute_lazy.py:470-472 does not guard it. But this is documented fail-loud design (review/04-exhaustive/raw/core.json:538: "_apply_column_renames leaves Polars to raise on rename target collisions (no silent fallback) — consistent with the repo's fail-loud philosophy") and aligns with CLAUDE.md ("Don't add unnecessary fallbacks; code should fail loudly"). tests/test_executor_builders.py:781 even feeds `{"a":"x","b":"x"}` as an accepted-by-design colliding config. So the backend half is a deliberate contract, not a defect, and the frontend authoring path that the finding blames is dead code.

The finding is refuted: the GroupedColumnsTab authoring path is unreachable (apiInput is in NO_COLUMNS_TAB; the only render site is the apiInput-only branch), and the backend's rename-collision-raises behavior is intentional fail-loud design pinned by tests. If anyone later re-enables a Columns/GroupedColumns tab for a node type AND wants to harden authoring, the surgical place would be stripGroupPrefix/toggleSegmentStrip in GroupedColumnsTab.tsx (it already has `allNames` at line 185) to skip or warn when a stripped target collides with an existing untouched column or another stripped target; but doing so now would be dead-code maintenance and would contradict the deliberate fail-loud contract.
refuted.repro_path: N/A (no repro written: finding is frontend-reachability; sub-claim confirmed inline)

refuted.title: ModellingPreview passes config={{}} to SummaryTab, silently dropping the user's MLflow experiment_name and model_name on export
